p.seg: Zǐ Lièzǐ lived in the countryside of Zhèng,
and for forty years, no one recognized him.
The ruler, ministers, and high officials of the state looked upon him
as one of the common people.
When the state was in financial straits,
he was about to be married off to Wèi.
His disciple said,
"Master, if you go, there will be no fixed return date.
Your disciple dares to ask something;
what will you teach when you go?
Has the Master not heard the words of Húqiū Zǐlín?"
Zǐ Lièzǐ laughed and said,
"What did Húzi say?"
However,
the Master once spoke to Bóhūn Màorén.
I overheard it,
and will try to tell it to you.
His words were:
"There is that which is born, and that which is not born.
There is that which transforms, and that which does not transform.
That which is not born can give birth to the born;
that which does not transform can transform the transforming.
That which is born cannot help but be born;
that which transforms cannot help but transform.
Therefore, there is constant birth and constant transformation.
That which is constantly born and constantly transformed
is born at every moment
and transforms at every moment.
Yin and Yang are like this,
the four seasons are like this.
That which is not born is suspected of being singular;
that which does not transform goes back and forth.
Going back and forth,
its boundaries cannot be exhausted.
Being suspected of being singular,
its way cannot be fathomed."
The *Huángdì Shū* says:
"The spirit of the valley never dies;
this is called the mysterious female.
The gate of the mysterious female
is called the root of Heaven and Earth.
Continuously it exists,
and its use is inexhaustible.
Therefore, that which gives birth to things is not born;
that which transforms things does not transform.
It is self-generating and self-transforming,
self-forming and self-coloring,
self-knowing and self-empowered,
self-diminishing and self-ceasing.
To call them birth and transformation, form and color, knowledge and power, diminishing and ceasing
is incorrect."
Zǐ Lièzǐ said:
"In the past, the sages used Yin and Yang to govern Heaven and Earth.
If that which has form is born from that which has no form,
then from where did Heaven and Earth arise?
Therefore, it is said:
There was *Tài Yì*,
there was *Tài Chū*,
there was *Tài Shǐ*,
there was *Tài Sù*.
*Tài Yì* is
when Qi has not yet appeared;
*Tài Chū* is
the beginning of Qi;
*Tài Shǐ* is
the beginning of form;
*Tài Sù* is
the beginning of substance.
When Qi, form, and substance are all present but not yet separated,
it is called Chaos.
Chaos means
that all things are mixed together and not yet separated.
Looking at it, you cannot see it;
listening to it, you cannot hear it;
feeling it, you cannot grasp it;
therefore, it is called *Yì*.
*Yì* has no boundaries;
*Yì* transforms into one,
one transforms into seven,
seven transforms into nine.
Nine is the ultimate
of the transformation of Qi;
then it transforms back into one.
One is
the beginning of the transformation of form.
That which is clear and light ascends to become Heaven;
that which is turbid and heavy descends to become Earth;
that which is harmonious Qi becomes human;
therefore, Heaven and Earth contain essence,
and the myriad things transform and are born."
Zǐ Lièzǐ said:
"Heaven and Earth do not have complete function,
sages do not have complete ability,
and the myriad things do not have complete use.
Therefore,
Heaven's function is to cover and nurture,
Earth's function is to shape and carry,
the sage's function is to teach and transform,
and things' function is to suit their nature.
Thus, Heaven has its shortcomings,
Earth has its strengths,
the sage has his impossibilities,
and things have their ways of communicating.
Why is this?
That which covers and nurtures cannot shape and carry;
that which shapes and carries cannot teach and transform;
that which teaches and transforms cannot go against what is suitable;
and that which is suitably determined cannot go beyond its position.
Therefore, the Way of Heaven and Earth
is either Yin or Yang;
the teachings of the sage
are either benevolence or righteousness;
and the suitability of the myriad things
is either gentle or strong:
all of these follow what is suitable and cannot go beyond their positions.
Therefore, there is that which is born,
and there is that which gives birth to the born;
there is that which has form,
and there is that which gives form to the formed;
there is that which has sound,
and there is that which gives sound to the sounded;
there is that which has color,
and there is that which gives color to the colored;
there is that which has taste,
and there is that which gives taste to the tasted.
That which gives birth to the born dies,
but that which gives birth to the born never ends;
that which gives form to the formed is solid,
but that which gives form to the formed never exists;
that which gives sound to the sounded is heard,
but that which gives sound to the sounded never emits;
that which gives color to the colored is visible,
but that which gives color to the colored is never apparent;
that which gives taste to the tasted is tasted,
but that which gives taste to the tasted is never presented:
all of these are functions of non-action.
It can be Yin, it can be Yang;
it can be gentle, it can be strong;
it can be short, it can be long;
it can be round, it can be square;
it can be alive, it can be dead;
it can be hot, it can be cool;
it can float, it can sink;
it can be *gōng*, it can be *shāng*;
it can go out, it can disappear;
it can be dark, it can be yellow;
it can be sweet, it can be bitter;
it can be fragrant, it can be stinky.
It has no knowledge,
it has no ability,
yet there is nothing it does not know,
and there is nothing it cannot do."
Zǐ Lièzǐ was going to Wèi,
and ate on the road.
A follower saw a hundred-year-old skull,
pulled up some weeds and pointed to it,
and turning to his disciple Bǎifēng said,
"Only you and I know that it has never been born and has never died.
Did this indulge in over-nourishment?
Did this indulge in excessive joy?
There are several kinds of seeds:
if *lài* turns into a quail,
if it gets water, it turns into *yì*,
if it gets the boundary between water and soil,
it turns into the clothes of *láipín*.
If it grows in a mound,
it turns into *língxì*.
If *língxì* gets a damp place to live,
it turns into *wūzú*.
The root of *wūzú* becomes a grub,
and its leaves become butterflies.
The butterfly
transforms into an insect,
which is born under the stove,
and its shape is like shedding,
and its name is *xiāduō*.
After a thousand days, *xiāduō*
transforms into a bird,
and its name is *gānyúgǔ*.
The foam of *gānyúgǔ* becomes *sīmí*.
*Sīmí* becomes the mouthparts of an vinegar fly.
The mouthparts of an vinegar fly give birth to yellow slime in vinegar,
and the yellow slime in vinegar gives birth to *jiǔyóu*.
*Jiǔyóu* gives birth to *màoruì*,
and *màoruì* gives birth to rotten maggots.
A sheep's liver transforms into a *dìgāo*,
the transformation of horse blood becomes *línyě*,
and human blood becomes wildfire.
The harrier transforms into a hawk,
the hawk transforms into a cuckoo,
and the cuckoo transforms back into a harrier.
The swallow transforms into a clam,
the field mouse transforms into a quail,
the rotten melon transforms into a fish,
the old leek transforms into amaranth,
the old ewe transforms into a monkey,
and fish eggs transform into insects.
The beasts of Dǎnyuán
become pregnant by themselves and give birth,
which are called *lèi*.
Birds of rivers and marshes are
conceived by sight and
called yì (鶂).
A purely female one is called dà yāo (大腰),
a purely male one is called zhì fēng (稺蜂).
A longing scholar is moved without a wife,
a longing woman is pregnant without a husband.
Hòu Jì (后稷) was born from a giant footprint,
Yī Yǐn (伊尹) was born from the hollow mulberry tree.
Jue Zhao (厥昭) was born from dampness.
Vinegar flies are born from wine.
Yáng Xī (羊奚) compares to bù sǔn (不筍).
Old bamboo produces qīng níng (青寧),
qīng níng (青寧) produces chéng (程),
chéng (程) produces horses,
horses produce humans.
Humans then return to the loom.
All things come from the loom,
and all return to the loom."
The *Huángdì Shū* (黃帝書) says:
"The movement of form does not produce form, but produces shadow;
the movement of sound does not produce sound, but produces echo;
the movement of nothingness does not produce nothingness, but produces something."
Form is something that must end,
will Heaven and Earth end?
They will end together with me.
Will the end advance?
I do not know.
The Dao ends in the fundamental absence of a beginning,
and advances in the fundamental absence of a further state.
That which has life returns to non-life,
that which has form returns to formlessness.
That which is not born,
is not fundamentally unborn;
that which is formless,
is not fundamentally formless.
That which has life
is something whose principle dictates it must end.
That which ends cannot but end,
just as that which has life cannot but have life.
To desire to perpetuate life
and exhaust its end
is to be deluded by numbers.
Spirit is
the *yòu* (又) of Heaven,
bones and skeletons are
the *yòu* (又) of Earth.
That which belongs to Heaven is clear and disperses,
that which belongs to Earth is turbid and gathers.
When spirit separates from form,
each returns to its true state;
therefore, it is called a ghost.
A ghost
is a return,
a return to its true home.
Huángdì (黃帝) said:
"When the spirit enters its gate,
and the bones return to their root,
what of me remains?"
From birth to death,
humans undergo four great transformations:
infancy,
youth,
old age,
and death.
In infancy,
one's qi (氣) is focused and the will is unified,
reaching the height of harmony;
things do not harm them,
virtue cannot be added to them.
In youth,
blood and qi (氣) overflow,
desires and thoughts arise in abundance;
things attack them,
and virtue therefore declines.
In old age,
desires and thoughts soften;
the body is about to rest,
and things no longer take precedence.
Although not as complete as in infancy,
compared to youth,
there is a gap.
In death,
they go to rest,
returning to their ultimate state.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) was traveling on Tài Shān (太山) when he saw Róng Qǐqī (榮啟期) walking in the fields of Chéng (郕),
wearing a deerskin coat and a rope belt,
playing the qín (琴) and singing.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) asked,
"Sir, what is the source of your joy?"
He replied,
"I have many sources of joy:
Heaven creates all things,
and humans alone are noble.
I have already been granted to be human,
this is one joy.
There is a distinction between male and female,
with men being honored and women being debased,
so men are considered noble;
I have already been granted to be male,
this is my second joy.
Some people are born and never see the sun and moon, and never leave their swaddling clothes,
but I am already ninety years old,
this is my third joy.
Poverty is the constant of scholars,
and death is the end of people,
dwelling in the constant and attaining the end,
what should I worry about?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
"Excellent!
He is able to ease his own mind."
Lín Lèi (林類) was nearly a hundred years old,
wearing a fur coat in late spring,
picking up dropped grains in the old fields,
singing and walking along.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) was heading to Wèi (衛) and saw him in the fields.
He turned to his disciples and said,
"That old man is worth talking to,
try going to ask him!"
Zǐgòng (子貢) requested to go.
He met him at the edge of the field,
faced him, and sighed,
"Sir, do you not regret
singing and picking up dropped grains?"
Lín Lèi (林類) continued walking,
and did not stop singing.
Zǐgòng (子貢) questioned him incessantly,
so he looked up and replied,
"What do I regret?"
Zǐgòng (子貢) said,
"When you were young, you were not diligent,
when you grew up, you did not compete for position,
and in old age, you have no wife or children,
and death is approaching:
what joy do you have in picking up dropped grains and singing?"
Lín Lèi (林類) laughed and said,
"What I find joy in,
everyone has,
but they instead take it as a worry.
Because I was not diligent when young,
and did not compete for position when grown up,
I have been able to live this long.
Because I have no wife or children in old age,
and death is approaching,
I am able to be so happy."
Zǐgòng (子貢) said,
"Longevity is what people desire,
and death is what people hate.
You find joy in death,
why?"
Lín Lèi (林類) said,
"Death and life
are a going and a returning.
Therefore, one who dies here,
how do we know they will not be born there?
Therefore, I know that they are not the same.
How do I know that eagerly seeking life is not a delusion?
And how do I know that my death now is not better than my life in the past?"
Zǐgòng (子貢) heard this,
did not understand his meaning,
and returned to tell Confucius.
Confucius said,
"I knew he could be talked to,
and indeed he was;
but he has attained it without fully understanding it."
Zǐgòng (子貢) was weary of learning
and said to Zhòngní (仲尼),
"I wish to rest."
Zhòngní (仲尼) said,
"Life has no rest."
Zǐgòng (子貢) said,
"Then is there nowhere for me, Cì (賜), to rest?"
Zhòngní (仲尼) said,
"There is indeed a place.
Look at the grave,
how level it is,
how orderly,
how mounded,
how separated,
and then you will know where to rest."
Zǐgòng (子貢) said,
"How great is death!
The gentleman rests there,
and the common man is laid to rest there."
Zhòngní (仲尼) said,
"Cì (賜)!
You understand it.
People all know the joy of life,
but do not know the suffering of life;
they know the weariness of old age,
but do not know the ease of old age;
they know the evil of death,
but do not know the rest of death."
Yàn Zǐ said:
"Excellent,
that the ancients had death!
The benevolent rest therein,
the unbenevolent are subdued therein."
Death is
the boundary of virtue.
The ancients called the dead returning people.
If we call the dead returning people,
then the living are travelers.
To travel without knowing to return
is to lose one's home.
If one person loses their home,
the world criticizes them;
if the world loses its home,
no one knows to criticize it.
If someone leaves their homeland,
abandons their close relatives,
neglects their family business,
and wanders in all directions without returning,
what kind of person is that?
The world would surely call them a reckless person.
If someone values the present age,
boasts of their cleverness and ability,
cultivates their reputation,
and exaggerates in the world
without knowing themselves,
what kind of person is that?
The world would surely consider them a wise and resourceful person.
These two
are both lost.
The world agrees with one but not the other,
only the sage knows what to agree with
and what to reject."
Someone said to Zǐ Lièzǐ:
"Why do you value emptiness?"
Lièzǐ said:
"Emptiness has no value."
Zǐ Lièzǐ said:
"If it is not its true name,
nothing is better than stillness,
nothing is better than emptiness.
Stillness and emptiness
allow one to attain their proper place;
taking and giving
cause one to lose their place.
After affairs are broken apart
do those who parade benevolence and righteousness arise,
but they cannot restore things."
Zhōu Xióng said:
"Movement and transformation never cease,
heaven and earth subtly shift,
who is aware of it?
Therefore, what is diminished there is increased here,
what is completed here is diminished there.
Diminishment and increase, completion and decay,
follow the world and follow death.
Coming and going connect with each other,
the intervals are too small to perceive,
who is aware of it?
No single breath progresses abruptly,
no single form decays abruptly;
one is not aware of its completion,
one is not aware of its decay.
It is like a person from youth to old age,
appearance, complexion, wisdom, and state
change without a day passing without alteration;
skin, nails, and hair
fall away following the world,
they are not like how they were in infancy and remain unchanged.
The intervals are imperceptible,
one waits until later to know."
There was a man from the state of Qǐ
who worried that the heavens and earth would collapse,
that he would have nowhere to rest his body,
and who stopped sleeping and eating.
There was also someone who worried about what he worried about,
so he went to explain it to him,
saying:
"Heaven
is merely accumulated air,
there is nowhere without air.
Like bending and stretching and breathing,
you spend all day walking and standing in the midst of the heavens,
why worry about it collapsing?"
The man said:
"If the heavens are indeed accumulated air,
won't the sun, moon, and stars fall?"
The one explaining it said:
"The sun, moon, and stars
are also merely luminous things within accumulated air;
even if they fall,
they cannot cause any harm."
The man said:
"What if the earth breaks?"
The one explaining said:
"The earth is merely accumulated clods,
filling up the four directions,
there is nowhere without clods.
Like pacing and treading,
you spend all day walking and standing on the earth,
why worry about it breaking?"
The man was greatly relieved and rejoiced,
and the one explaining it was also greatly relieved and rejoiced.
Chánglú Zǐ heard this and laughed, saying:
"Rainbows,
clouds and mist,
wind and rain,
and the four seasons,
these are the accumulation of air that forms the heavens.
Mountains,
rivers and seas,
metal and stone,
fire and wood,
these are the accumulation of form that forms the earth.
To know accumulated air
and to know accumulated clods,
how can you say they won't break?
Heaven and earth
are but a tiny object in the void,
the largest of things within existence.
They are difficult to end and difficult to fathom,
this is certainly so;
they are difficult to measure and difficult to know, this is certainly so.
To worry about them breaking
is truly too far;
to say they won't break
is also not right.
Heaven and earth cannot avoid breaking,
and will eventually return to breaking.
When they encounter the time of breaking,
why wouldn't you worry?"
Zǐ Lièzǐ heard this and laughed, saying:
"To say that heaven and earth will break is also wrong,
to say that heaven and earth will not break is also wrong.
Whether they break or not,
is something I cannot know.
However,
that is one,
this is one.
Therefore, living, we do not know death,
dying, we do not know life;
coming, we do not know going,
going, we do not know coming.
Whether they break or not,
how could I concern myself with it?"
Shùn asked Zhēng:
"Can the Dao be attained and possessed?"
He said:
"Your body is not yours to possess,
how can you possess the Dao?"
Shùn said:
"If my body is not mine to possess,
who possesses it?"
He said:
"It is what heaven and earth entrust with form.
Life is not yours to possess,
it is what heaven and earth entrust with harmony.
Nature and destiny are not yours to possess,
it is what heaven and earth entrust with compliance.
Grandchildren are not yours to possess,
it is what heaven and earth entrust with renewal.
Therefore, walking, you do not know where you are going,
dwelling, you do not know what you are holding onto,
eating, you do not know why you are doing so.
Heaven and earth
are forceful and bright, they are qi;
how can they be possessed?"
In the state of Qí, the Guóshì family was very wealthy,
while in the state of Sòng, the Xiàngshì family was very poor.
From Sòng to Qí,
they asked for the method.
Guóshì told them:
"I am good at being a thief.
When I started being a thief,
in one year I had enough,
in two years I was satisfied,
in three years I had a large estate.
From then on,
I extended my help to the villages."
Xiàngshì was overjoyed.
He understood the words about being a thief,
but did not understand the Dao of being a thief,
so he climbed over walls and dug through rooms,
whatever his hands and eyes could reach,
he did not fail to seize.
Before long,
he was convicted of theft,
and his family's previous wealth was confiscated.
Xiàngshì thought that Guóshì had misled him,
and went to complain to him.
Guóshì said:
"How did you go about being a thief?"
Xiàngshì told him the details.
Guóshì said:
"Alas!
Have you lost the Dao of being a thief to this extent?
Now I will tell you.
I have heard that heaven has its seasons,
and the earth has its advantages.
I steal the timely benefits of Heaven and Earth,
the copious moisture of clouds and rain,
the produced and nurtured resources of mountains and marshes,
to grow my grain,
to plant my crops,
to build my walls,
to construct my house.
On land I steal birds and beasts,
in the water I steal fish and turtles;
there is nothing that is not stolen.
Now, grain, crops, earth, wood, birds, beasts, fish, and turtles
are all produced by Heaven,
how could they be my possessions?
Yet I steal from Heaven and suffer no disaster.
But gold, jade, precious jewels, grains, silks, wealth, and goods,
that people accumulate,
are these given by Heaven?
If one is convicted for stealing these,
who is there to complain to?"
Xiàng Shì was greatly perplexed,
thinking that the importance of Guó Shì overwhelmed him,
so he went to Dōngguō Xiānshēng to ask about it.
Dōngguō Xiānshēng said:
"Is not your own person a thief?
You steal the harmony of Yīn and Yáng to complete your life,
and carry your form;
how much more so external things are not stolen?
Truly,
Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things are inseparable;
to claim possession is
all delusion.
The stealing of Guó Shì is
impartial,
therefore there is no disaster;
your stealing
is selfish,
therefore you are condemned.
To have impartiality and selfishness
is also stealing;
to lack impartiality and selfishness
is also stealing.
Impartiality in impartiality, selfishness in selfishness,
this is the virtue of Heaven and Earth.
He who knows the virtue of Heaven and Earth,
who is a thief?
Who is not a thief?"
After Huángdì ascended the throne for fifteen years,
pleased that the world supported him,
he nourished his life,
pleased his ears and eyes,
and gratified his nose and mouth,
until his skin was parched and his complexion darkened and muddied,
and his five emotions were confused and bewildered.
After another fifteen years,
worried that the world was not well-governed,
he exhausted his intelligence,
advanced his mental strength,
and managed the people,
until his skin was parched and his complexion darkened and muddied,
and his five emotions were confused and bewildered.
Huángdì then sighed and exclaimed:
"My excess has been excessive!
Nourishing myself alone is such a problem,
governing the myriad things is such a problem!"
Thereupon, he relinquished myriad affairs,
abandoned his palace chambers,
dismissed his personal attendants,
removed the hanging bells,
reduced his kitchen provisions,
and retreated to live in seclusion in the grand hall,
purifying his mind and regulating his form,
for three months not attending to matters of state.
He slept during the day and dreamed
of traveling to the land of the Huáxū Shì.
The land of the Huáxū Shì is west of Yǎnzhōu
and north of Táizhōu,
I do not know how many tens of millions of *lǐ* this country is;
it cannot be reached by boat or carriage, or by the strength of feet,
but only by spiritual travel.
In that country, there are no teachers or leaders,
it is simply natural.
Its people have no desires,
it is simply natural.
They do not know to rejoice in life,
they do not know to abhor death,
therefore there are no premature deaths;
they do not know to be close to themselves,
they do not know to alienate things,
therefore there is no love or hate;
they do not know opposition,
they do not know compliance,
therefore there are no advantages or disadvantages:
they have no love or hate,
they have no fear or dread.
Entering water, they do not drown;
entering fire, they are not burned.
Being hacked or struck causes no pain,
being poked or prodded causes no itching.
Riding the air is like treading on solid ground,
sleeping in emptiness is like lying on a bed.
Clouds and mist do not obstruct their sight,
thunder and lightning do not disrupt their hearing,
beauty and ugliness do not disturb their minds,
mountains and valleys do not hinder their steps,
they travel spiritually.
When Huángdì awoke,
he was pleased and content,
and summoned Tiānlǎo, Lìmù, and Tàishān Jī,
and told them, saying:
"I have lived in seclusion for three months,
purifying my mind and regulating my form,
thinking of a way to nourish myself and govern things,
but I did not obtain the method.
Tired, I slept,
and dreamed as such;
now I know that the ultimate *dào* cannot be sought with emotions.
I know it!
I have attained it!
But I cannot tell it to you."
After another twenty-eight years,
the world was greatly governed,
nearly like the land of the Huáxū Shì,
and the emperor ascended on high.
The people mourned for him,
and for more than two hundred years they did not cease.
Mount Liègūshè is in the midst of the Sea hé continent.
On the mountain, there is a divine person
who inhales the wind and drinks the dew,
and does not eat the five grains;
his heart is like a deep spring,
his form is like a virgin;
he does not lean on or love anyone,
and immortals and sages are his subjects;
he does not fear or get angry,
and sincere and respectful people are his servants;
he does not bestow or grant favors,
yet things are naturally sufficient;
he does not gather or collect,
yet he has no fault.
Yīn and Yáng are always in harmony,
the sun and moon are always bright,
the four seasons are always constant,
wind and rain are always balanced,
reproduction and nurture are always timely,
and the year's harvests are always abundant;
and the soil has no damage,
people have no premature deaths or evils,
things have no blemishes or pestilence,
and ghosts have no spiritual influence there.
Lièzǐ studied with Lǎoshāng Shì
and befriended Bó Gāozi;
he advanced the *dào* of these two men
and returned riding the wind.
Yǐn Shēng heard of this,
and followed Lièzǐ to live with him,
and for several months did not return home.
Taking advantage of a moment, he asked to be taught his skills,
but ten times he asked and ten times he was not told.
Yǐn Shēng resented this and asked to leave,
but Lièzǐ did not allow it.
Yǐn Shēng left.
After several months,
his intention did not cease,
and he went to follow him again.
Lièzǐ said:
"Why do you come and go so frequently?"
Yǐn Shēng said:
"Previously, Zhang Dài had a request of you,
but you did not tell me,
and I harbored a resentment towards you.
Now I have shaken it off,
and that is why I have come again."
Lièzǐ said:
"Before, I thought you were enlightened,
but now your baseness has reached this point?
Alas!
I will tell you what I learned from my teacher.
Since I served my teacher and befriended such men,
after three years,
my heart dared not think of right and wrong,
and my mouth dared not speak of profit and harm,
and I only gained one glance from my teacher.
After five years,
my heart began to think of right and wrong,
and my mouth began to speak of profit and harm,
and my teacher began to show a smile on his face.
After seven years,
whatever I thought in my heart
had no right or wrong;
whatever I said from my mouth
had no benefit or harm.
The master then started to invite me to sit beside him on the mat.
After nine years,
whatever I thought in my mind,
whatever I spoke from my mouth,
I did not know whether I was right or wrong, beneficial or harmful,
nor did I know whether others were right or wrong, beneficial or harmful;
nor did I know that the master was my teacher,
or other people were my friends.
Inside and outside advanced.
And then the eyes were like the ears,
the ears were like the nose,
the nose was like the mouth,
nothing was different.
The mind congealed and the body released,
flesh and bones all melted away;
unaware of where my body leaned,
or where my feet trod,
following the wind east and west,
like a dry leaf or empty husk.
I simply did not know whether the wind was riding me?
Or I was riding the wind?
Now you live in the master's door,
but it has not yet been a full period,
and you have resentment and regret again and again.
Your small body will be rejected by the qi,
your single node will not be carried by the earth.
To tread emptiness and ride the wind,
how is that almost possible?"
Yǐn Shēng was very ashamed,
held his breath for a long time,
and dared not speak again.
Lièzǐ asked Guān Yǐn, saying:
"The perfect man can walk unseen,
tread on fire without feeling hot,
walk above all things without trembling.
May I ask how to reach this state?"
Guān Yǐn said:
"This is the guarding of pure qi,
not something that can be achieved by wisdom, skill, courage, or boldness.
Jī,
I will tell you:
all that have forms, appearances, sounds, or colors,
are things.
How can things be far apart from each other?
How can they be enough to reach the first?
It is only color.
Then the thing is created from the formless,
and stops at the point where it cannot be transformed.
If one obtains this and exhausts it,
how can things be able to stop it?
He will dwell in the measure of not being deep,
and hide in the un-ended discipline,
wandering in the place where all things end and begin.
Unify his nature,
nourish his qi,
contain his virtue,
in order to communicate with the creation of things.
If one is like this,
his heavenly guard is complete,
his spirit has no gaps,
how can things enter him?
A drunken man falling from a carriage,
though quickly, does not die.
His bones and joints are the same as others,
but the harm he suffers is different from others,
because his spirit is complete.
He does not know when he is riding,
nor does he know when he is falling.
Death, life, alarm, and fear do not enter his chest,
therefore he encounters things without being afraid.
He obtains completeness from wine
and is still like this,
how much more so when he obtains completeness from Heaven?
The sage is hidden in Heaven,
therefore things cannot harm him."
Liè Yǔkòu was shooting for Bó Hūn Wúrén,
drawing the bow to its fullest extent,
placing a cup of water on his elbow,
and releasing the arrow.
The arrow after arrow followed each other,
and square arrows fell into square spaces.
At this time,
he was like a wooden figure.
Bó Hūn Wúrén said:
"This is the shooting of shooting,
not the shooting of not shooting.
Should I go with you to climb high mountains,
tread on dangerous rocks,
and overlook a hundred-fathom abyss,
would you be able to shoot?"
Thereupon Wúrén ascended a high mountain,
trod on a dangerous rock,
and overlooked a hundred-fathom abyss.
Turning his back,
two-tenths of his foot hung outside.
He bowed to Yǔkòu and urged him forward.
Yǔkòu fell to the ground,
sweat flowing to his heels.
Bó Hūn Wúrén said:
"The perfect man
looks up to the blue sky,
and down into the yellow springs,
waves away to the eight extremes,
and his spirit and qi do not change.
Now you are fearful and have a startled gaze,
your inner self is in danger!"
Fàn Shì had a son named Zǐ Huá,
who was good at cultivating his private reputation,
and the whole country admired him.
He was favored by the Jìn ruler,
and though he did not hold office, he was ranked above the three ministers.
What his eyes preferred to look at,
the Jìn country honored.
What his mouth preferred to eat,
the Jìn country removed.
Those who walked in his courtyard were equal to those in the court.
Zǐ Huá made his knights
attack each other with their intelligence and base,
and the strong bullied the weak.
Even if they were wounded and broken in front,
he did not care.
He spent the whole day and night taking this as amusement and pleasure,
and the country almost became accustomed to it.
Hé Shēng and Zǐ Bó were the top guests of the Fàn family.
On their way out, passing through the outskirts,
they stayed overnight at the house of the field worker Shāngqiū Kāi.
In the middle of the night,
Hé Shēng and Zǐ Bó were talking to each other about Zǐ Huá's name and power,
which could make the living die,
and the dead live;
make the rich poor,
and the poor rich.
Shāngqiū Kāi, who had previously been in distress due to hunger and cold,
secretly listened from behind the north window.
Therefore, he borrowed grain and carried a basket to Zǐ Huá's door.
Zǐ Huá's disciples were all from noble families,
wearing white clothes and riding in carriages,
walking slowly and looking broadly.
Seeing Shāngqiū Kāi was old and weak,
with a dark face,
and his clothing was not neat,
none of them did not despise him.
Then they humiliated and deceived him,
pushing, pulling, shoving, and hitting,
doing everything.
Shāngqiū Kāi always had a calm expression,
but the skills of the guests were simple,
and they became tired of the teasing and laughter.
So they rode with Shāngqiū Kāi to a high platform,
and said casually in the crowd:
"Anyone who can throw themselves down will be rewarded with a hundred gold pieces."
Everyone competed to respond.
Shāngqiū Kāi believed it was true,
and then threw himself down first,
his form like a flying bird,
landing on the ground,
his bones and joints without a scratch.
The Fàn family's party thought it was accidental,
and were not surprised.
Then they pointed to the lewd corner of the river bend and said:
"There is a treasure pearl in there,
you can get it by swimming."
Shāngqiū Kāi then followed and swam in it.
After coming out,
he indeed obtained the pearl.
Everyone began to doubt.
Zǐ Huá then ordered that he be put in the order of those who were provided with meat and silk clothes.
Suddenly, the Fàn family's storage caught a big fire.
Zǐ Huá said:
"If anyone can enter the fire to take out the brocade,
they will be rewarded according to the amount they obtain."
Shāngqiū Kāi went
without difficulty,
entering the fire and returning,
without dust on him,
and his body unburned.
The Fàn family's party thought he had the Dao,
so they apologized together and said:
"We did not know that you had the Dao and ridiculed you,
we did not know that you were a divine man and insulted you.
You are fooling us,
you are deaf to us,
you are blind to us.
May we ask for your Dao?"
Shāngqiū Kāi said:
"I have no Dao.
Even my heart,
does not know why it is so.
However,
I have one thing here,
I will try to tell you."
Formerly, two guests stayed at my house,
and I heard praises of the power of the Fàn Shì family,
that they could cause the surviving to perish,
and the perished to survive;
the rich to become poor,
and the poor to become rich.
I truly had no divided heart,
therefore I came from afar.
When I arrived,
I thought the words of your faction were all true,
and I only feared that my sincerity would not be sufficient,
and my actions would not be timely enough.
I did not know where to place my form and body,
nor where my benefit or harm lay.
My heart was single-minded.
Nothing went against my wishes;
that was all.
Now I know that your faction deceived me.
I hide suspicion within,
and outwardly I am wary of observation and judgment.
I retroactively hope I did not drown in the past,
and now I am burning with anxiety,
trembling with fear.
How can water and fire be approached again?"
From that time on,
when the Fàn Shì disciples encountered beggar-children or horse-doctors on the road,
they did not dare to insult them,
but would certainly get out of their carriages and salute them.
Zǎi Wǒ heard of this
and told Zhòng Ní.
Zhòng Ní said,
"Do you not understand?
The most sincere person
can move things.
Moving Heaven and Earth,
affecting ghosts and spirits,
traversing the universe without encountering resistance –
how could they only tread on danger
and enter water and fire?
Shāngqiū Kāi's counterfeit object was not rejected,
how much more so when we are both sincere?
Young man, remember this!"
The head herdsman of King Zhōu Xuānwáng
had a servant named Liáng Yāng,
who could raise wild birds and beasts,
feeding them in the garden and courtyard.
Even tigers, wolves, eagles, and ospreys
were all gentle and docile.
The males and females were in front,
breeding and multiplying in groups.
Different species lived together,
not fighting or biting each other.
The king worried that his skill would end with his life,
so he ordered Máo Qiūyuán to transmit it.
Liáng Yāng said,
"Yāng is a lowly servant,
what skill can I tell you?
I fear that the king thinks I am hiding something from you,
so I will simply tell you my method of raising tigers.
Generally, if you comply with them, they are happy;
if you go against them, they are angry.
This is the nature of those with blood and qi.
But how could happiness and anger be expressed randomly?
They are all caused by offenses against them.
When feeding tigers,
one does not dare to give them live animals,
because they will be angry at killing them;
one does not dare to give them whole animals,
because they will be angry at tearing them apart.
Know their hunger and fullness,
understand their angry heart.
Although tigers and humans are different species,
they are pleased with those who nourish them,
which is compliance;
therefore, those who kill them are acting against them.
Therefore, how dare I act against them and make them angry?
Nor do I comply with them to make them happy.
For the return of happiness is certainly anger,
and the return of anger is often happiness,
and both are not moderate.
Now, my heart has no compliance or resistance,
so the birds and beasts see me
as their equal.
Therefore, those who roam my garden
do not think of high forests and vast marshes;
those who sleep in my courtyard
do not desire deep mountains and secluded valleys;
that is the way it is."
Yán Huí asked Zhòng Ní, saying,
"I once crossed the deep abyss of Shāng Shēn,
and the ferryman's skill in handling the boat was like that of a god.
I asked him,
saying,
'Can boat handling be learned?'
He said,
'Yes;
those who can swim can be taught,
and those who are good at swimming can do it quickly.
As for those who have never seen a boat and suddenly try to handle it.'
I asked him, and he did not tell me.
May I ask what he meant?"
Zhòng Ní said,
"Ah!
I have been examining its writing with you for a long time,
and have not yet understood its true meaning,
but let me explain it.
Those who can swim can be taught,
because they take water lightly;
those who are good at swimming can do it quickly,
because they forget about the water.
As for those who have never seen a boat and suddenly try to handle it,
they see the abyss as a hill,
and the overturning of the boat as the overturning of their cart.
With overturning and reversing happening before them,
they cannot enter their abode.
Where can they go without leisure?
One who digs with a tile is skillful,
one who digs with a hook is fearful,
and one who digs with gold is dazed.
The skill is the same,
but having something to be proud of
makes one value external things.
Those who value external things are clumsy internally."
Kǒngzǐ was observing the Lüliáng waterfalls,
where the suspended water was thirty *rèn* high,
and the spray flowed for thirty *lǐ*.
Turtles, crocodiles, fish, and turtles could not swim there.
He saw a man swimming there.
He thought that he was someone suffering and wanting to die,
so he ordered his disciples to go downstream and catch him.
After several hundred paces, he came out,
with his hair disheveled and singing,
and he was swimming in the Táng River.
Kǒngzǐ followed him and asked him, saying,
"The Lüliáng suspended water is thirty *rèn* high,
and the spray flows for thirty *lǐ*.
Turtles, crocodiles, fish, and turtles cannot swim there.
Earlier, I saw you swimming there.
I thought that you were someone suffering and wanting to die,
so I ordered my disciples to go downstream to catch you.
You came out with your hair disheveled and singing,
and I took you for a ghost.
But upon closer inspection, you are a man.
May I ask if there is a way to tread water?"
He said,
"No,
I have no way.
I began with habit,
grew with nature,
and achieved with destiny.
I enter with the current,
and exit with the waves.
I follow the way of the water and do not act for my own sake.
This is how I navigate it."
Kǒngzǐ said,
"What does it mean to begin with habit,
grow with nature,
and achieve with destiny?"
He said,
"I was born on the hills and feel at ease on the hills;
that is habit.
I grew up in the water and feel at ease in the water;
that is nature.
I do not know why I am like this;
that is destiny."
Zhòng Ní went to Chǔ.
Coming out of a forest,
he saw a hunchbacked old man catching cicadas,
as if he were picking them up.
Zhòng Ní said,
"You are skilled!
Do you have a method?"
He said,
"I have a method.
In the fifth and sixth months, if I balance two pellets on top of each other without them falling,
then I lose only a little;
if I balance three without them falling,
then I lose one in ten;
if I balance five without them falling,
it is as if I am picking them up.
When I stand,
I am like a stump;
when I hold my arm, it is like a withered branch.
Although Heaven and Earth are vast and all things are many,
I only know the cicada's wings.
I do not turn back or to the side,
and I do not exchange the cicada's wings for all things.
Why would I not succeed?"
Kǒngzǐ turned to his disciples and said,
"When one focuses one's will without distraction,
one can approach the divine.
He is talking about this hunchbacked old man!"
The old man said,
"You are a bunch of scholars dressed in clothes,
how would you know to ask about this?
Cultivate what you should be cultivating,
and then discuss it."
A man who lived by the sea was fond of gulls;
every morning he went to the sea,
and played with the gulls.
The gulls would gather by the hundreds and wouldn't stop.
His father said:
"I hear that the gulls all play with you;
catch some and bring them here,
I want to play with them."
The next day he went to the sea,
but the gulls danced in the air and did not come down.
Therefore it is said:
The ultimate expression transcends words,
the ultimate action is non-action.
What limited intelligence can comprehend
is shallow indeed.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ led an army of a hundred thousand
to hunt in Zhōngshān,
burning the undergrowth and the forests,
the flames spreading for a hundred *lǐ*.
A man emerged from a stone cliff,
rising and falling with the smoke and embers.
The crowd thought it was a ghost or spirit.
After the fire passed,
he walked out slowly,
as if he had not been through anything.
Xiāngzǐ was surprised and detained him,
examining him closely:
his form, features, and orifices
were those of a man;
his breath and voice
were those of a man.
He asked by what means he could dwell in stone
and enter fire.
The man said:
"What thing do you call stone?
What thing do you call fire?"
Xiāngzǐ said:
"That from which you just emerged
is stone;
that through which you just walked
is fire."
The man said:
"I do not know."
Wèi Wénhóu heard of this and
asked Zǐxià, saying:
"Who is this man?"
Zǐxià said:
"According to what I, Shāng, have heard from the Master,
one who is in harmony is greatly united with things,
and things can cause him no harm or obstruction;
he can roam through metal and stone,
and tread on water and fire,
all with ease."
Wénhóu said:
"Why don't you, my son, do this?"
Zǐxià said:
"To empty the heart and cast away wisdom,
I, Shāng, am not yet capable of that.
However,
I can try to speak of it when I have the time."
Wénhóu said:
"Why doesn't the Master do this?"
Zǐxià said:
"The Master is capable of it, but he is capable of not doing it."
Wénhóu was greatly pleased.
There was a divine shaman who came from Qí to live in Zhèng,
named Jì Xián,
who knew people's life, death, survival, ruin, fortune, and lifespan,
predicting them by year, month, ten-day period, and day,
like a god.
The people of Zhèng, seeing him,
all avoided him and ran away.
Lièzǐ was entranced by him
and returned to tell Húqiūzǐ,
saying:
"I originally thought the Master's Way was ultimate,
but there is something even more ultimate."
Húzǐ said:
"I and you have not grasped its form,
nor exhausted its substance,
and yet you are sure you have obtained the Way?
With many females and no male,
how can there be eggs?
If you use the Way to resist the world,
you are sure to be believed.
That is why you allow others to observe you.
Try bringing him here
and showing him to me."
The next day,
Lièzǐ brought him to see Húzǐ.
He came out and said to Lièzǐ:
"Alas!
Your teacher is dead,
he will not live,
he cannot last ten days.
I see something strange,
I see damp ashes."
Lièzǐ went in,
tears soaking his collar,
and told Húzǐ.
Húzǐ said:
"Just now I showed him the earth's pattern,
sprouting from the unceasing stillness;
he probably saw my budding virtue.
Try bringing him again!"
The next day,
he brought him again to see Húzǐ.
He came out and said to Lièzǐ:
"Fortunately,
your teacher has met me,
he has a chance of recovery.
The ashes faintly show life;
I saw his blocked potential."
Lièzǐ went in and told Húzǐ.
Húzǐ said:
"Just now I showed him the heavenly framework,
where names and realities do not enter,
and its workings originate from the heel;
this is called blocked potential.
He probably saw the beginnings of my goodness.
Try bringing him again!"
The next day,
he brought him again to see Húzǐ.
He came out and said to Lièzǐ:
"Your teacher
is unsettled within,
I cannot read him.
Have him settle himself,
and then I will try to read him again."
Lièzǐ went in and told Húzǐ.
Húzǐ said:
"Just now I showed him the Great Void, without sign or trace;
he probably saw the balance of my vital force.
The turning of a minnow creates a whirlpool,
the stilling of water creates a whirlpool,
the flowing of water creates a whirlpool,
the flooding of water creates a whirlpool,
the eddying of water creates a whirlpool,
the gushing of water creates a whirlpool,
the converging of water creates a whirlpool,
the rushing of water creates a whirlpool,
the overflowing of water creates a whirlpool;
these are the nine whirlpools.
Try bringing him again!"
The next day,
he brought him again to see Húzǐ.
Before he had even stood still,
he lost himself and ran away.
Húzǐ said:
"Chase him!"
Lièzǐ chased him but could not catch up,
and returned to report to Húzǐ,
saying:
"He has vanished,
he is lost,
I could not catch him."
Húzǐ said:
"Just now I showed him that which has not yet emerged from my source.
I met him with emptiness and yielding,
not knowing who or what he was;
he followed me in confusion,
he followed me like a wave;
that is why he fled."
After this, Lièzǐ considered himself to have never begun learning, and he returned home.
For three years he did not go out,
he cooked for his wife,
he fed the pigs as he would people,
he had no preferences in his affairs,
he discarded ornamentation and returned to simplicity,
standing alone like a clod of earth;
he was like a confused person, yet whole,
and remained so until the end of his days.
When Zǐ Lièzǐ was going to Qí,
he turned back midway,
and met Bóhūn Màorén.
Bóhūn Màorén said:
"Why are you turning back?"
He said:
"I was startled."
"What startled you?"
He said:
"I ate at ten soup shops,
and five of them served me before others."
Bóhūn Màorén said:
"If that is so, why should you be startled by this?"
He said:
"If one's inner sincerity is not resolved,
one's outward appearance will betray the light within,
and one will use external things to pacify people's hearts,
causing them to slight the old and respect the young,
and to disregard what troubles them."
Now, the broth seller makes a special effort to sell his soup,
leaving a great surplus;
the profit is meager,
and the authority is slight,
yet he still does this.
How much more so the lord of ten thousand chariots,
who labors for the state
and exhausts his wisdom on affairs!
He will entrust me with affairs
and expect me to perform meritorious service;
this is why I am alarmed."
Bóhūn Màoren said:
"Excellent observation!
If you remain aloof,
people will protect you."
Before long he went to visit,
and the shoes outside the door were numerous.
Bóhūn Màoren stood facing north,
leaning on his cane, pressing it against his chin.
After standing for a while,
he left without a word.
The guest informed Lièzǐ.
Lièzǐ grabbed his shoes and ran barefoot,
reaching the door
and asking:
"Now that you have come, Master,
might you not offer some instruction?"
He said:
"Enough!
I told you long ago that
people would protect you,
and indeed they are protecting you.
It is not that you can make people protect you,
but that you cannot prevent people from protecting you.
Why then this affectation?
Affectation invites the bizarre.
Moreover, there is bound to be affectation;
if you are swayed and act on it,
it is pointless;
those who associate with you
will not tell you.
What they say in private
is all poison to people.
No one is aware, no one understands;
how can they judge what is suitable?"
Yáng Zhū went south to Pèi,
and Lǎodān traveled west to Qín,
meeting him on the outskirts.
Reaching Liáng, he encountered Lǎozǐ.
Lǎozǐ stopped on the road, looked up at the sky, and sighed, saying:
"I thought you were teachable at first,
but now you are unteachable."
Yángzǐ did not answer.
Arriving at the lodging,
he offered water for rinsing, a towel, and a comb,
took off his shoes outside the door,
and crawled forward on his knees, saying:
"Just now, Master, you looked up at the sky and sighed, saying:
'I thought you were teachable at first,
but now you are unteachable.'
Your disciple wanted to ask for your explanation,
but you were still on the road,
and so I dared not.
Now that you are at leisure, Master,
may I ask what my fault is?"
Lǎozǐ said:
"You stare
and gawk,
who can abide with you?
Great purity seems like disgrace,
abundant virtue seems insufficient."
Yáng Zhū was startled and changed his expression, saying:
"I respectfully hear your instruction."
When he went to the lodging,
the host welcomed him and his family,
the master held the mat,
the wife held the towel and comb;
the lodgers vacated their seats,
and those tending the fire avoided the stove.
When he returned,
the lodgers were vying with him for a seat.
Yáng Zhū passed through Sòng and headed east to an inn.
The innkeeper had two concubines,
one beautiful,
the other ugly;
the ugly one was favored and the beautiful one despised.
Yángzǐ asked the reason.
The innkeeper's boy replied:
"The beautiful one considers herself beautiful;
I do not recognize her beauty;
the ugly one considers herself ugly;
I do not recognize her ugliness."
Yángzǐ said:
"My disciples, remember this!
If you practice virtue and discard the practice of considering yourself virtuous,
where can you go and not be loved?"
In the world, there is a way to constant victory,
and there is a way to inconstant victory.
The way to constant victory is called gentleness,
the way to constant defeat is called strength.
People know these two things,
but they do not truly understand them.
Therefore, the ancients said:
"Strength
precedes not resembling oneself,
gentleness precedes emerging from oneself."
Preceding not resembling oneself,
reaching resemblance to oneself,
is perilous.
Preceding emerging from oneself,
there is no peril.
Using this to overcome oneself is like moving pawns,
using this to manage the world is like moving pawns,
meaning not overcoming yet self-overcoming,
not managing yet self-managing.
Zhōuzǐ said:
"If you desire strength,
you must safeguard it with gentleness;
if you desire might,
you must preserve it with weakness.
Accumulation of gentleness inevitably leads to strength,
accumulation of weakness inevitably leads to might.
Observe that which accumulates,
and you will know the direction of misfortune and fortune.
Might overcoming those not resembling oneself,
reaching resemblance to oneself is strength;
gentleness overcoming that which emerges from oneself,
its power is immeasurable."
Lǎodān said:
"Armies that are strong are destroyed,
trees that are stiff are broken.
The gentle and weak are companions of life,
the firm and strong are companions of death."
Appearance need not be childlike
for intelligence to be childlike,
intelligence need not be childlike
for appearance to be childlike.
The sage takes childlike intelligence and abandons the childlike appearance,
the masses are drawn to the childlike appearance and neglect childlike intelligence.
Those whose appearance is childlike like mine,
I draw near and love;
those whose appearance is different from mine,
I distance myself from and fear.
Having a seven-foot frame,
different hands and feet,
wearing hair and containing teeth,
leaning and walking,
we call them humans;
but humans may well have the heart of a beast.
Even if they have the heart of a beast,
they are treated as kin because of their appearance.
Bearing wings and wearing horns,
having divided teeth and spread claws,
flying above and running below,
we call them birds and beasts;
but birds and beasts may well have the heart of a human.
Even if they have the heart of a human,
they are treated as strangers because of their appearance.
Páo Xīshì, Nǚwāshì, Shénnóngshì, Xià Hòushì,
had serpent bodies and human faces,
ox heads and tiger noses:
these had appearances not of humans,
but had the virtue of great sages.
Xià Jié, Yīn Zhòu, Lǔ Huán, Chǔ Mù,
had appearances with seven orifices,
all the same as humans,
but had the hearts of beasts.
Thus, if the masses cling to a single appearance to seek perfect wisdom,
success is unlikely.
Huángdì and Yándì fought at the field of Bǎnquán,
leading bears, grizzlies, wolves, leopards, wildcats, and tigers as the vanguard,
with eagles, hazel grouses, hawks, and kites as banners,
this was using the power of birds and beasts.
Yáo charged Kuí to oversee the music,
striking stone and patting stone,
and the hundred beasts all danced;
when the Xiāo Sháo was played nine times,
the phoenixes came to court:
this was using sound to attract birds and beasts.
In that case, the hearts of birds and beasts,
how are they different from humans?
Their forms and sounds are different from humans,
and we do not know the way to connect with them.
The sage knows everything,
understands everything,
and so is able to draw them near and use them.
The intelligence of birds and beasts has a natural component that is the same as that of humans;
they all desire to preserve life,
and do not need to borrow intelligence from humans:
males and females pair,
mothers and children are affectionate;
they avoid the flat and rely on the steep,
they shun the cold and seek the warmth;
when dwelling, they gather in groups,
when moving, they march in ranks;
the small ones stay inside,
the strong ones stay outside;
when drinking, they help each other,
when eating, they call out to the group.
In the ancient times,
they lived together with humans,
and walked alongside them.
During the time of emperors and kings,
they began to be startled, frightened, and scattered.
By the later ages,
they hid and fled,
in order to avoid trouble and harm.
Now, in the eastern state of Jièshì,
there are people who can frequently understand the languages of the six domestic animals;
this is probably due to a partial understanding.
The divinely wise people of ancient times
fully understood the feelings and states of all things,
and completely understood the sounds of different kinds.
They gathered them together,
instructed them and received their teachings,
treating them the same as people.
Therefore, they first gathered ghosts and spirits and chīmèi (魑魅),
then reached out to people from all directions,
and finally gathered birds and beasts, insects and moths.
They said that creatures with blood and breath
did not differ much in intelligence.
The divinely wise knew this,
so there were no omissions in what they taught.
In Sòng, there was a keeper of monkeys (jūgōng)
who loved monkeys;
he raised them in groups,
and could understand the monkeys' intentions;
the monkeys also understood the keeper's heart.
He reduced his family's rations
to satisfy the monkeys' desires.
Soon he was impoverished
and was going to limit their food.
Fearing that the monkeys would not be obedient to him,
he first deceived them, saying:
"I will give you acorns,
three in the morning and four in the evening,
is that enough?"
All the monkeys rose up and were angry.
After a while, he said:
"I will give you acorns,
four in the morning and three in the evening,
is that enough?"
All the monkeys bowed down and were pleased.
Creatures that use their limited intelligence to control each other
are all like this.
Sages who use their wisdom to control the masses of fools
are just like the monkey keeper who uses his wisdom to control the monkeys.
The substance of the matter is not diminished,
yet they are made to be happy or angry!
Jì Shěngzi (紀渻子) was raising fighting chickens for King Xuān of Zhōu (Zhōu Xuānwáng).
After ten days, the king asked,
"Can the chicken fight yet?"
He replied,
"Not yet;
it is still arrogant and relies on its qi (氣, vital energy)."
Ten days later, he asked again.
He replied,
"Not yet;
it still responds to shadows and echoes."
Ten days later, he asked again.
He replied,
"Not yet;
it still glares and is full of vigor."
Ten days later, he asked again.
He replied,
"Almost.
Even though other chickens crow,
it is no longer affected.
It looks like a wooden chicken.
Its virtue is complete.
Other chickens dare not respond;
they just run away."
Huì Āng (惠盎) met with King Kāng of Sòng (Sòng Kāngwáng).
King Kāng stamped his feet and cleared his throat,
and said quickly,
"What I like
is courage and strength,
I don't like those who advocate benevolence and righteousness.
What will you teach me, guest?"
Huì Āng replied,
"I have a way here
to make people, though brave,
unable to be pierced;
though strong,
unable to be hit.
Does Your Majesty not have any interest in this?"
The King of Sòng said,
"Good;
this is what I want to hear."
Huì Āng said,
"But to be unable to be pierced or hit
is still a disgrace.
I have a way here
to make people, though brave, not dare to stab;
though strong, not dare to strike.
Not daring
is not because they lack the will to do so.
I have a way here
to make people fundamentally lack the will to do so.
Lacking the will
means there is no heart of love and benefit.
I have a way here
to make all the men and women in the world
happily want to love and benefit him.
This is more virtuous than courage and strength,
exceeding them fourfold.
Does Your Majesty not have any interest in this?"
The King of Sòng said,
"This is what I want to obtain."
Huì Āng replied,
"It is Kǒng (孔) and Mò (墨).
Kǒng Qiū (孔丘) and Mò Dí (墨翟)
have no territory to be rulers,
no official position to be leaders;
yet all the men and women in the world
stretch their necks and stand on tiptoe, hoping to be made secure and benefited by them.
Now, Your Majesty
is the ruler of ten thousand chariots;
if you truly have this ambition,
then everyone within your four borders
will receive its benefits.
Your virtue will far exceed that of Kǒng and Mò."
The King of Sòng had nothing to say in response.
Huì Āng hurried out.
The King of Sòng said to his attendants,
"Eloquently put;
the guest has persuaded me with his words!"
During the time of King Mù of Zhōu (Zhōu Mùwáng),
a transformed person (huà rén) came from the westernmost country,
who could enter water and fire,
pierce metal and stone;
reverse mountains and rivers,
move cities and towns;
ride in the void without falling,
and touch solid things without hindrance.
He could transform in countless ways,
without end.
Having already changed the forms of things,
he could also alter people's thoughts.
King Mù respected him as a god,
and served him as a ruler.
He offered his palace bedroom for him to live in,
provided the three sacrificial animals for him to eat,
and selected female musicians to entertain him.
The transformed person thought that the king's palace was lowly and not fit to live in,
that the king's food was tainted and not fit to eat,
and that the king's concubines were smelly and not fit to be near.
So King Mù rebuilt for him.
The work of earth and wood,
the colors of red and white,
left nothing to be desired in craftsmanship.
The five treasuries were emptied,
and the terrace began to be built.
It was a thousand *rèn* (仞, ancient unit of length) high,
overlooking Mount Zhōngnán (終南),
and was called the Terrace Reaching the Sky (Zhōngtiān zhī Tái, 中天之臺).
He selected the most beautiful, graceful, and charming virgins from Zhèng (鄭) and Wèi (衛),
who applied fragrant oils,
carefully painted their eyebrows,
wore hairpins and earrings,
dressed in fine silk,
and dragged long silk skirts.
They powdered their faces white, darkened their eyebrows,
wore jade pendants and rings,
mixed artemisia and *ròuxiāng* (若香, a fragrant orchid) to fill the air,
and played the *Chéngyún* (承雲), *Liùyíng* (六瑩), *Jiǔsháo* (九韶), and *Chénlù* (晨露) to entertain him.
Every month, they offered jade clothing,
and every day, they presented jade food.
The transformed person was still not satisfied and only reluctantly visited it.
After living there for only a short time,
he asked the king to travel with him.
The king held onto the transformed person's sleeve,
and they soared upwards, stopping only in mid-air.
They arrived at the transformed person's palace.
The transformed person's palace was constructed of gold and silver,
adorned with pearls and jade;
it rose above the clouds and rain, and one could not see what supported it below,
appearing like gathered clouds.
What the eyes and ears saw and heard,
what the nose and mouth tasted and smelled,
were all things not found in the human world.
The king truly believed that it was Qīngdū (清都), Zǐwēi (紫微), Jūntiān (鈞天), and Guǎnglè (廣樂),
the places where the Emperor resided.
The king looked down and saw that his palace and pavilions resembled piles of mud and grass.
The king felt as if he had lived there for decades and did not miss his kingdom.
The transformed person again asked the king to travel with him,
and wherever they went,
they could not see the sun and moon above,
nor the rivers and seas below.
The light and shadow were so dazzling that
the king's eyes were blurred and he could not see;
the sounds were so overwhelming that
the king's ears were confused and he could not hear.
His hundreds of bones and six viscera
trembled and could not be still.
His mind was lost and his essence depleted,
and he begged the conjurer to bring him back.
The conjurer moved him,
and the king felt as if he had collapsed.
When he awoke,
the place where he sat was still the same as before,
and the attendants were still the same people as before.
He looked ahead,
and the wine was not yet clear,
and the delicacies were not yet cold.
The king asked where he had come from.
The attendants on the left and right said,
"Your Majesty was merely lost in thought."
Because of this, Mù Wáng was beside himself for three months before recovering.
He questioned the conjurer again.
The conjurer said,
"I wandered with Your Majesty in spirit;
how could the body have moved?
Moreover, the place where we stayed before,
how is it different from Your Majesty's palace?
The places we wandered before,
how are they different from Your Majesty's gardens?
Your Majesty sometimes has moments of leisure, and doubts are momentarily forgotten.
The extremes of transformation,
the intervals between slowness and speed,
how can they be fully grasped?"
The king was greatly pleased.
He did not care about state affairs,
nor did he enjoy his concubines,
and he indulged in distant travels.
He ordered that his eight steeds be harnessed,
with *quánliú* on the right and *lǜěr* on the left,
with *chìjì* on the right and *báiqiān* on the left as outriders.
The king rode in the chariot with Zào Fù as his driver,
and *qíshuāng* as his lancer;
in the next chariot,
*qúhuáng* was on the right and *yúlún* on the left,
with *dàolí* on the left and *shānzǐ* on the right as outriders,
Bǎi Yāo drove the chariot,
with Cān Bǎi as his driver,
and Bēn Róng as his lancer.
They galloped thousands of *lǐ*
and arrived at the country of the Jù Sōu clan.
The Jù Sōu clan offered the blood of white swans to the king to drink,
and provided the milk of cattle and horses to wash the king's feet,
as well as the feet of the people in the two chariots.
After drinking and continuing their journey,
they spent the night on the slopes of Kūnlún,
on the northern bank of the Red River (*Chì Shuǐ*).
The next day, they ascended the hills of Kūnlún
to view the palace of the Yellow Emperor (*Huángdì*);
and sealed it
to leave to later generations.
Then he was entertained by Xī Wángmǔ and feasted above the Jade Pool (*Yáo Chí*).
Xī Wángmǔ sang a song for the king,
and the king responded in kind,
the words of which were mournful.
He watched the sunset in the west.
He traveled ten thousand *lǐ* in a day.
Then the king sighed and said,
"Alas!
I, the one man, am not full of virtue but indulge in pleasure.
Will later generations count my transgressions!"
Mù Wáng was almost a divine being!
He was able to exhaust the pleasures of his lifetime,
yet he passed away after a hundred years,
and the world thought he had ascended to immortality.
Lǎo Chéngzǐ studied illusion with Yǐn Wén Xiānshēng,
but for three years he was not told anything.
Lǎo Chéngzǐ asked about his faults and sought to withdraw.
Yǐn Wén Xiānshēng bowed and invited him into the room.
He dismissed his attendants and spoke to him, saying:
"In the past, when Lǎo Dān was going west,
he turned and told me, saying:
'The energy of life,
the form of existence,
all is illusion.
What the Creator begins,
what *yīn* and *yáng* transform,
is called life,
and is called death.
Exhausting numbers and achieving change,
transforming and changing according to form,
is called transformation,
and is called illusion.
The Creator's craftsmanship is ingenious,
and His work is profound,
so it is difficult to exhaust and difficult to end.
What follows form has obvious skill,
and its work is shallow,
so it arises and disappears quickly.
Knowing that illusion and transformation are no different from life and death,
only then can one begin to study illusion.
You and I are also illusions;
why is there a need to study it?'"
Lǎo Chéngzǐ returned,
and using the words of Yǐn Wén Xiānshēng,
he pondered deeply for three months;
and then he was able to exist and disappear at will,
and alter the four seasons;
to create thunder in winter,
and create ice in summer.
What flies walks,
and what walks flies.
He never wrote down his techniques,
so they were never passed on to the world.
Zǐ Lièzǐ said:
"Those who are good at transformation,
their ways are secretive and obscure,
and their achievements are the same as ordinary people.
The virtue of the Five Emperors (*Wǔ Dì*),
and the achievements of the Three Kings (*Sān Wáng*),
did not necessarily exhaust their wisdom and courage,
but were perhaps achieved through transformation.
Who can fathom it?"
Awakening has eight signs,
and dreams have six indications.
What are the eight signs?
First is the past,
second is action,
third is attainment,
fourth is loss,
fifth is sorrow,
sixth is joy,
seventh is life,
and eighth is death.
These eight signs
are what the body encounters.
What are the six indications?
First is the true dream,
second is the fright dream,
third is the thought dream,
fourth is the waking dream,
fifth is the joyful dream,
and sixth is the fearful dream.
These six are
what the spirit interacts with.
Those who do not understand the origin of feelings and changes,
when things happen, are confused about the reason for it;
those who understand the origin of feelings and changes,
when things happen, know the reason for it.
Knowing the reason for it, then there is nothing to fear.
The waxing and waning, diminishing and growing of a single body
are all connected to heaven and earth,
and correspond to the categories of things.
Therefore, when *yīn* energy is strong,
one dreams of wading through great waters and being afraid;
when *yáng* energy is strong,
one dreams of wading through great fires and being burned;
when both *yīn* and *yáng* are strong,
one dreams of killing.
When one is very full, one dreams of giving;
when one is very hungry, one dreams of taking.
Therefore, those who have a disease of floating emptiness
dream of flying;
those who have a disease of sinking solidity
dream of drowning.
Sleeping with a belt on
one dreams of snakes,
and a bird carrying hair
one dreams of flying.
Approaching *yīn* dreams of fire,
and approaching illness dreams of food.
Drinking wine makes one worry,
and singing and dancing makes one cry.
Zǐ Lièzǐ said:
"The spirit's encounters are dreams,
and the body's encounters are events,
so daytime thoughts become nighttime dreams,
where spirit and form meet.
Therefore, when the spirit is concentrated, thoughts and dreams naturally disappear.
Believe in awakening and do not speak,
believe in dreams and do not relate them;
they are the coming and going of the transformations of things.
The true people of ancient times,
when awake, forgot themselves,
and when sleeping, did not dream;
how close to empty words!"
In the southernmost corner of the Western Pole is a country
that does not know where its borders lie,
called the country of Gǔ Mǎng.
The energies of *yīn* and *yáng* do not interact there,
so there is no distinction between cold and heat;
the light of the sun and moon does not shine there,
so there is no distinction between day and night.
Its people do not eat or wear clothes, and sleep a lot.
They wake up once every fifty days,
believing that what they do in their dreams is real,
and that what they see when they are awake is false.
The land where the four seas meet is called the Central Kingdom (Zhōngyāng zhī Guó),
spanning the north and south of the Hé River,
crossing the east and west of Mount Dài,
over ten thousand *lǐ*.
Its *yīn* and *yáng* are carefully measured,
thus there is one cold and one hot season;
the distinction between dusk and dawn is clearly observed,
thus there is one day and one night.
Its people have both wisdom and foolishness.
All things flourish,
and talents and skills are diverse.
There are rulers and ministers overseeing each other,
and rites and laws upholding each other.
The things they do
cannot be counted.
One waking and one sleeping,
they believe that what is done while awake is real,
and what is seen in dreams is false.
In the northern corner of the easternmost region, there is a country
called the Fùluò zhī Guó.
Its land's air is always warm,
illuminated by the remaining light of the sun and moon. Its land
does not produce fine crops.
Its people eat grass roots and tree fruits,
do not know how to cook with fire,
are by nature fierce and brave,
the strong and weak rely on each other,
value victory and do not esteem righteousness;
they often run about,
seldom rest,
and are always awake and never sleep.
Yǐn Shì of Zhōu greatly managed his property,
and those below him who were engaged as servants
worked from early morning until dark without rest.
There was an old servant
whose strength was exhausted,
but he was made to work even harder.
During the day he groaned and sighed while attending to his duties,
and at night he was tired and fell into a deep sleep.
His spirit scattered and dissipated,
and every night he dreamed of being a ruler of a state.
Residing above the people,
managing the affairs of the entire state.
Feasting and enjoying himself in palaces and towers,
indulging in whatever he desired,
his joy was unparalleled.
When he woke up, he resumed his service.
Someone sympathized with his diligence.
The servant said:
"Life is a hundred years,
divided into day and night.
During the day I am a servant,
and it is indeed bitter;
at night I am a ruler,
and my joy is unparalleled.
What is there to complain about?"
Yǐn Shì focused his mind on worldly affairs,
and worried deeply about his family's business,
so both his mind and body were exhausted,
and at night he was also tired and fell asleep.
Every night he dreamed of being a servant,
running and toiling,
doing everything;
frequently scolded and beaten,
nothing was spared.
He mumbled and groaned in his sleep,
sighing until dawn.
Yǐn Shì was troubled by this,
and consulted his friend.
The friend said:
"Your position is sufficient to bring you honor,
and your wealth is abundant,
far surpassing others.
Dreaming of being a servant at night
is merely the alternation of hardship and ease,
a common occurrence.
If you want to experience both wakefulness and dreams,
how can that be possible?"
Yǐn Shì heard his friend's words,
reduced the workload of his servants,
lessened his own worries and thoughts,
and his illness gradually subsided.
A man from Zhèng was gathering firewood in the fields,
when he encountered a startled deer,
chased and struck it,
killing it.
Fearing that others would see it,
he quickly hid it in a ditch,
covering it with banana leaves.
He could not contain his joy.
Soon after, he forgot where he had hidden it,
and then thought it was a dream.
He walked along the road, chanting about the event.
A person nearby heard him,
used his words and took the deer.
After returning home,
he told his family:
"Earlier, a firewood gatherer dreamed of getting a deer but didn't know where it was;
I have now obtained it,
he truly was only dreaming."
His family said:
"Are you then saying that it was the firewood gatherer's dream that you got the deer?
Was there even a firewood gatherer?
Now that we have really obtained the deer,
is your dream then true?"
The man said:
"I am certain that I got the deer,
why would I need to know if he dreamed or if I dreamed?"
When the firewood gatherer returned,
he was not happy about losing the deer.
That night he truly dreamed of the place where he had hidden it,
and also dreamed of the person who had obtained it.
At dawn,
he followed his dream and found it.
They then sued and argued over it,
and brought it to the judge.
The judge said:
"You first truly obtained the deer,
but wrongly thought it was a dream;
you truly dreamed of obtaining the deer,
but wrongly thought it was real.
He truly took your deer,
and is now arguing with you over the deer.
His family also said it was a dream that he took the deer,
and that no one got the deer.
Now that we have this deer,
let's divide it between the two of you."
He reported this to the ruler of Zhèng.
The ruler of Zhèng said:
"Alas!
Is the judge going to dream of dividing the deer between them?"
He consulted the prime minister.
The prime minister said:
"Whether it is a dream or not,
your servant cannot distinguish.
If you wish to distinguish between being awake and dreaming,
only Huángdì and Kǒng Qiū can.
Now that Huángdì and Kǒng Qiū are gone,
who can distinguish it?
It is best to follow what the judge says."
Sòng Yánglǐ Huázi
suffered from forgetfulness in middle age,
forgetting in the evening what he had taken in the morning,
and forgetting in the morning what he had given in the evening;
on the road he would forget to walk,
and in the house he would forget to sit;
he did not recognize the past,
and he did not recognize the present.
His whole family hated him.
They consulted a historian and divined,
but the divination did not work;
they consulted a shaman and prayed,
but it was ineffective;
they consulted a doctor and treated him,
but he did not recover.
There was a Confucian scholar from Lǔ
who recommended himself as able to cure him,
and Huázi's wife and children offered half of their property to request his method.
The Confucian scholar said:
"This is certainly not something that can be divined by divination,
not something that can be prayed for through supplication,
not something that can be treated with medicine.
I will try to transform his mind,
change his thoughts,
and perhaps he will recover!"
Thereupon, he tried exposing him to the cold and then asked for clothes;
starving him and then asked for food;
confining him in darkness and then asked for light.
The Confucian scholar happily told his son:
"The disease can be cured.
However, my method is secret, passed down through generations,
and not to be told to others.
Try dismissing those around him,
and staying alone with him in a room for seven days." They followed his advice.
No one knew what he was doing,
but the illness of many years
was completely cured in one morning.
Once Huázi regained his senses, he was very angry,
banished his wife, punished his children,
and wielding a spear, chased the Confucian scholar away.
The people of Sòng seized him and asked the reason.
Huázi said:
"In the past, when I was forgetful,
I was carefree, not aware of whether heaven and earth existed or not.
Now, I suddenly recognize
the past, and in the past decades, the existence and destruction, gains and losses,
sorrows and joys, likes and dislikes,
myriad thoughts arise in confusion.
I fear that the future existence and destruction, gains and losses, sorrows and joys, likes and dislikes will disturb my mind in this way,
and that a moment of forgetfulness
cannot be regained?"
Zǐgòng heard of this and was puzzled,
and told Kǒngzǐ about it.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"This is not something you can understand!"
He turned to Yán Huí and said, "Remember this."
A person from Qín ān (秦人 Féngshì) had a son,
who was intelligent when young,
but as he grew older, he developed a disease of confusion.
He heard singing and thought it was weeping,
he saw white and thought it was black,
he smelled fragrant things and thought they were rotten,
he tasted sweet things and thought they were bitter,
he did wrong and thought it was right:
wherever his mind went,
heaven and earth, the four directions, water and fire, cold and heat,
all were upside down and in disorder.
Yángshì (楊氏) said to his father,
"Many gentlemen in Lǔ (魯) possess skills and arts;
perhaps they can cure him?
Why don't you go and consult them?"
His father went to Lǔ (魯),
passing through Chén (陳),
where he met Lǎodān (老聃),
and told him about his son's condition.
Lǎodān (老聃) said,
"How can you know that your son is confused?
Today, everyone in the world
is confused about right and wrong,
and deluded about benefit and harm.
Many suffer from the same disease,
so naturally no one notices.
Besides, the confusion of one person
is not enough to overturn a family,
the confusion of one family
is not enough to overturn a village,
the confusion of one village
is not enough to overturn a state,
the confusion of one state
is not enough to overturn the world.
If the whole world is confused,
who can correct it?
If everyone in the world
had the same mind as your son,
then you would be the one who is confused.
Joy and sorrow, sound and color, smell and taste, right and wrong,
who could correct them?
Moreover, these words of mine might themselves be confused,
how much more so the gentlemen of Lǔ (魯),
who are even more deeply confused;
how could they possibly resolve the confusion of others?
Spare your provisions,
you would be better off returning home quickly."
A man from Yàn (燕) was born in Yàn (燕),
grew up in Chǔ (楚),
and returned to his native state when he was old.
Passing through the state of Jìn (晉),
his traveling companion deceived him;
pointing at a city, he said,
"This is the city of Yàn (燕)."
The man's expression changed with sorrow.
Pointing at a local shrine, he said,
"This is the shrine of your village."
Then he sighed deeply.
Pointing at a house, he said,
"This is the dwelling of your ancestors."
Then he wept quietly.
Pointing at a grave mound, he said,
"This is the tomb of your ancestors."
The man could not restrain his crying.
His traveling companion burst out laughing,
and said,
"I was deceiving you just now;
this is the state of Jìn (晉)."
The man felt great shame.
When he arrived in Yàn (燕),
and truly saw the cities and shrines of Yàn (燕),
and truly saw the dwellings and tombs of his ancestors,
his sorrow became even fainter.
Zhòngní (仲尼) was at leisure,
Zǐgòng (子貢) entered to attend him,
and had a worried expression.
Zǐgòng (子貢) did not dare to ask,
and went out to tell Yánhuí (顏回).
Yánhuí (顏回) took up his zither and sang.
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) heard it,
and indeed summoned Huí (回) to enter,
and asked,
"Why are you alone happy?"
Huí (回) said,
"Why are you alone worried?"
Kǒngzǐ (孔子) said,
