only concerned with the affairs
and having no time to think about death.
Then how could our lord have obtained this position and be standing here?
Because they alternately occupied it,
alternately left it,
until it came to Your Lordship,
yet you alone weep for it,
this is unkind.
I see an unkind lord,
I see flattering ministers.
Seeing these two,
is why I alone secretly laugh."
Jǐng Gōng was ashamed,
raised his cup and punished himself.
He punished the two ministers
each with two cups.
Among the people of Wèi, there was one named Dōngmén Wú,
whose son died, but he did not grieve.
His steward said:
"Your love for your son
is unparalleled in the world.
Now that your son has died and you do not grieve,
why is this?"
Dōngmén Wú said:
"I was often without a son,
and I did not grieve when I had no son.
Now that my son has died,
it is the same as when I had no son before,
why should I grieve?"
Farmers rush to the seasons,
merchants pursue profit,
artisans chase skills,
officials pursue power;
power makes it so.
However, farmers have floods and droughts,
merchants have gains and losses,
artisans have successes and failures,
officials have fortunes and misfortunes;
fate makes it so.
Yáng Zhū was traveling in Lǔ,
staying at the house of the Mèng family.
The head of the Mèng family asked, saying:
"Man is simply man,
why seek fame?"
He said:
"Those who seek fame do so for wealth."
"Having become wealthy,
why not stop there?"
He said:
"To seek nobility."
"Having become noble,
why not stop there?"
He said:
"To prepare for death."
"Having died,
what is it for?"
He said:
"For the sake of one's descendants."
"What benefit does fame bring to descendants?"
He said:
"Fame is to torment one's body,
scorch one's heart.
Those who ride on fame,
their beneficence extends to their clan,
their benefit encompasses their village;
how much more so their descendants?"
"All who seek fame must be incorruptible,
and incorruptibility leads to poverty;
those who seek fame must yield,
and yielding leads to lowliness."
He said:
"When Guǎn Zhòng was minister of Qí,
if the ruler was lewd, he was lewd as well;
if the ruler was extravagant, he was extravagant as well.
His will matched the ruler's words,
his way was carried out, and the state became hegemon.
After his death,
he was merely Guǎn Zhòng.
When the Tián family was minister of Qí,
if the ruler was full, he humbled himself;
if the ruler was stingy, he gave to the people.
The people all turned to him,
and he eventually possessed the state of Qí;
his descendants enjoy it,
and have not been cut off even to this day."
"Thus, true fame leads to poverty,
false fame leads to wealth."
He said:
"In reality, there is no fame;
in fame, there is no reality.
Fame
is merely falsehood.
In the past, Yáo and Shùn falsely yielded the empire to Xǔ Yóu and Shàn Juǎn,
yet did not lose the empire,
and enjoyed their reigns for a hundred years.
Bó Yí and Shū Qí truly yielded the throne of Gūzhú,
and ultimately lost their state,
starving to death on Shǒuyáng Mountain.
The distinction between reality and falsehood
is as clear as this."
Yáng Zhū said:
"A hundred years is the greatest lifespan,
and few among a thousand attain a hundred years.
Even if there is one,
from infancy to decrepit old age,
nearly half of it is spent.
The time spent resting in sleep at night,
and the time spent unaware during the day, again nearly half of it is spent.
The pain of illness, the sorrow of grief,
loss, and fearful anxiety,
again nearly half of it is spent.
Measuring among these ten-odd years,
the moments of leisurely contentment
without a single worry,
are but a single moment.
Then what is the purpose of man's life?
What joy is there?
It is for fine food and drink,
for sounds and sights.
Yet fine food and drink cannot always satiate,
and sounds and sights cannot always be enjoyed.
Furthermore, one is restricted and encouraged by punishments and rewards,
advanced and retreated by fame and laws;
restlessly striving for fleeting, empty praise,
planning for posthumous glory;
meekly conforming to the views of the ears and eyes,
cherishing one's physical self over what is right and wrong;
vainly losing the ultimate joy of the present,
unable to indulge oneself in the moment.
Heavy prisoners in shackles,
how are they different?
People of the remote past
knew that life is a temporary arrival,
knew that death is a temporary departure;
therefore they followed their hearts and acted,
not going against what nature favors;
the pleasures of the present life
are not to be rejected,
therefore they are not persuaded by fame.
They roamed following their nature,
not opposing what all things favor;
the name after death
is not to be sought,
therefore they are not reached by punishments.
The precedence of reputation,
the length of years,
are not to be measured.
Yáng Zhū said:
"What all things differ in is life,
what they have in common is death.
In life there are the wise and foolish, the noble and lowly;
this is where they differ.
In death there is decay and annihilation;
this is what they have in common.
However,
wisdom and foolishness, nobility and lowliness
are not something we can control,
decay and annihilation
are also not something we can control.
Therefore, life is not something we bring about,
death is not something we cause;
wisdom is not something we make wise,
foolishness is not something we make foolish,
nobility is not something we make noble,
lowliness is not something we make lowly.
Yet all things are born and die equally,
are wise and foolish equally,
are noble and lowly equally.
Ten years is death,
a hundred years is death.
The benevolent sage is death,
the fierce fool is death.
In life, one is Yáo and Shùn,
in death, they are rotten bones;
in life, one is Jié and Zhòu,
in death, they are rotten bones.
Rotten bones are all the same,
who can tell the difference?
Just enjoy the present life,
why worry about after death?"
Yáng Zhū said:
" Bó Yí did not want to die,
but he clung to purity,
and starved to death.
Zhǎn Jì did not want to be without affection,
but he clung to chastity,
and ended up with few descendants.
The mistakes of purity and chastity are so bad!"
Yáng Zhū said:
" Yuán Xiàn was poor in Lǔ,
Zǐ Gòng accumulated wealth in Wèi.
Yuán Xiàn's poverty harmed his life,
Zǐ Gòng's wealth accumulation burdened his body."
"So poverty is not acceptable,
nor is wealth accumulation acceptable;
where then is acceptability to be found?"
He said:
"Acceptability is found in enjoying life,
acceptability is found in relaxing the body.
Therefore, one who is good at enjoying life is not poor,
one who is good at relaxing the body does not accumulate wealth."
Yáng Zhū said:
"There is an ancient saying:
'In life, we sympathize with each other,
in death, we abandon each other.'
This saying is most profound.
The way of sympathizing with each other
is not only about affection;
diligence can bring comfort,
hunger can bring fullness,
cold can bring warmth,
poverty can bring success.
The way of abandoning each other
is not about not feeling sorrow;
it is about not including pearls and jade,
not wearing patterned brocade,
not presenting sacrifices,
not setting out funerary objects.
Yàn Píngzhòng asked Guǎn Yíwú about nourishing life.
Guǎn Yíwú said:
'Let it be,
do not block or obstruct it.'
Yàn Píngzhòng said:
'What does that mean?'
Yíwú said:
'Let the ears listen to what they want to hear,
let the eyes see what they want to see,
let the nose smell what it wants to smell,
let the mouth say what it wants to say,
let the body be comfortable as it wants,
let the mind do what it wants to do.
The ears want to hear sounds,
but if they cannot hear,
it is called obstructing hearing;
the eyes want to see beautiful sights,
but if they cannot see,
it is called obstructing sight;
the nose wants to smell pepper and orchids,
but if it cannot smell them,
it is called obstructing scent;
the mouth wants to speak about right and wrong,
but if it cannot speak,
it is called obstructing wisdom;
the body wants comfort and richness,
but if it cannot have them,
it is called obstructing ease;
the mind wants freedom and ease,
but if it cannot do it,
it is called obstructing nature.
All these obstructions
are the masters of ruin and abuse.
Remove the masters of ruin and abuse,
and happily await death;
one day, one month,
one year, ten years,
this is what I call nourishing life.
Confine these masters of ruin and abuse,
cling to them and not let go,
anxiously living for a long time, a hundred years,
a thousand years, ten thousand years,
this is not what I call nourishing life.'
Guǎn Yíwú said:
'I have already told you about nourishing life,
what about seeing off the dead?'
Yàn Píngzhòng said:
'Seeing off the dead is simple,
what shall I tell you?'
Guǎn Yíwú said:
'I would like to hear about it.'
Píngzhòng said:
'Once dead,
how is it up to me?
Burning the body is fine,
drowning the body is fine,
burying the body is fine,
exposing the body is fine,
wrapping it in firewood and discarding it in a ditch is fine,
wrapping it in fine embroidered clothes and placing it in a stone coffin is fine,
it depends on what happens.'
Guǎn Yíwú turned and said to Bào Shū and Huáng Zǐ:
'The way of life and death,
the two of us have advanced in it.'"
Zǐchǎn was the prime minister of Zhèng,
and controlled the government; for three years,
the good obeyed his transformations,
the wicked feared his prohibitions,
and the state of Zhèng became well-governed.
The feudal lords dreaded him.
He had an elder brother named Gōngsūn Cháo,
and a younger brother named Gōngsūn Mù.
Cháo loved wine,
Mù loved women.
In Cháo's house,
thousands of jugs of wine were piled up,
and fermented grains formed mounds;
a hundred steps from the gate,
the smell of mash and dregs assaulted one's nose.
When he was lost in wine,
he knew nothing of the safety and danger of the world,
the regrets of human affairs,
the presence or absence of things in his house,
the closeness or distance of his nine clans,
the sorrow or joy of existence.
Even if water, fire, weapons, and blades were crossing in front of him,
he would not know.
Mù's back courtyard
had dozens of chambers,
all filled with carefully selected young and beautiful women.
When he was absorbed in lust,
he kept away from relatives,
cut off friendships,
and hid in the back courtyard,
spending the days and nights there;
he came out only once every three months,
and even then, he was not satisfied.
If there were beautiful unmarried women in the villages,
he would bribe people to get them,
and use matchmakers to entice them;
he would not stop until he had obtained them.
Zǐchǎn worried about this day and night,
and secretly consulted with Dèng Xī, saying:
"Qiáo has heard that governing oneself extends to governing the family,
and governing the family extends to governing the state.
This saying goes from near to far.
Qiáo can govern the state well,
but my family is in chaos.
Is the path reversed?
What method should I use to save my two sons?
Please advise them!"
Dèng Xī said:
"I have been wondering about this for a long time,
but I dared not speak first.
Why don't you seize the opportunity to teach them,
explain the importance of life,
and entice them with the honor of rites and righteousness?"
Zǐchǎn used Dèng Xī's words,
and took the opportunity to visit his brothers, and told them:
"What makes humans superior to animals is intelligence.
What intelligence leads to is rites and righteousness.
When rites and righteousness are established, fame and position will come.
If you act on emotions
and indulge in desires,
then your life will be in danger.
If you accept Qiáo's words,
you will regret it in the morning and receive your salary in the evening."
Cháo Mù said:
"I have known this for a long time,
and I have been considering it for a long time.
Why would I wait for your words to understand it?
It is difficult to encounter life
and easy to reach death.
Using the difficult-to-encounter life
to wait for the easy-to-reach death,
what is there to think about?
You want to respect rites and righteousness to show off to others,
and feign emotions to attract fame.
I think this is worse than death.
I want to enjoy all the pleasures of this life
and exhaust the joys of my years.
My only concern is that my stomach will be full and I won't be able to drink as much as I want,
or that I will be exhausted and unable to indulge in sex;
I have no time to worry about the ugliness of my reputation
or the danger to my life.
Furthermore, you boast with your ability to govern the state,
and want to confuse my mind with rhetoric,
and please my heart with glory and wealth.
Isn't that despicable and pathetic?
I also want to tell you something else.
Those who are good at governing externally
may not govern things well,
and their bodies suffer;
those who are good at governing internally
may not cause chaos,
and their nature is at ease.
With your external governance,
your laws may be temporarily implemented in one state,
but they do not accord with the hearts of the people;
with my internal governance,
it can be extended to the whole world,
and the way of ruler and subject will cease.
I have always wanted to use this method to enlighten you,
but you are teaching me with that method instead?"
Zǐchǎn was at a loss for words.
Another day, he told Dèng Xī.
Dèng Xī said:
"You live with a true man but do not know it.
Who would call you wise?
The governance of Zhèng Guó is accidental,
not your achievement."
Wèi Duānmù Shū was
a descendant of Zǐgòng.
Relying on his ancestors' wealth,
his family accumulated tens of thousands of gold.
He did not manage worldly affairs
and indulged in what he liked.
What the people wanted to do
and what people wanted to play with,
he did everything
and played with everything.
Walls, houses, terraces,
gardens, ponds,
food, drink, carriages, clothes,
music, and concubines
were comparable to the rulers of Qí and Chǔ.
As for what his feelings desired,
what his ears wanted to hear,
what his eyes wanted to see,
what his mouth wanted to taste,
even if they were from remote foreign countries
and not produced in the land of Qí,
he would obtain them without fail;
they were like things within his fence.
As for his travels,
even if the mountains and rivers were steep and dangerous,
and the roads were long and far,
he would go there without fail,
as if he were walking a short distance.
Hundreds of guests stayed in his courtyard every day,
and the kitchen
never stopped cooking,
and the halls
never stopped playing music.
After providing for himself,
he first distributed the remainder to his clan;
after providing for his clan,
he then distributed the remainder to his village;
after providing for his village,
he then distributed the remainder to the whole country.
When he was sixty years old
and his energy was declining,
he abandoned his family affairs
and distributed all his treasures, jewels, carriages, clothes, and concubines.
He finished it all in one year
and did not leave any wealth for his descendants.
When he was sick,
he had no medicine in store;
when he died,
he had no money for burial.
The people of the country
who had received his charity
contributed to bury him
and returned the wealth to his descendants.
Qín Gǔlí heard of this and said:
"Duānmù Shū is a madman
who has disgraced his ancestors."
Duàn Gānmù heard of this and said:
"Mù Shū is a wise man
whose virtue exceeds his ancestors.
What he did
and what he accomplished
were based on his intentions
and what he truly believed in.
The gentlemen of Wèi mostly restrain themselves with rites and teachings,
which is not enough to understand this man's heart."
Mèngsūn Yáng asked Yángzǐ:
"If there is a person here
who values life and loves his body
and wants not to die,
is that possible?"
He said:
"It is impossible to avoid death in principle."
"What about wanting to live longer?"
He said:
"It is impossible to live longer in principle.
Life cannot be preserved by valuing it,
nor can the body be strengthened by loving it.
Besides, what is the point of living longer?
The five emotions of likes and dislikes
are the same in ancient times as they are now;
the well-being of the four limbs
is the same in ancient times as it is now;
the joys and sorrows of the world
are the same in ancient times as they are now;
the changes of order and chaos
are the same in ancient times as they are now.
Having heard it,
having seen it,
having experienced it,
a hundred years is still too much,
let alone the suffering of living longer?"
Mèngsūn Yáng said:
"If that's the case,
dying quickly is better than living longer;
then stepping on sharp blades
and entering boiling water
would achieve one's will."
Yángzǐ said:
"No;
once born,
then abandon and entrust yourself to it,
pursue what you desire,
and wait for death.
When about to die,
then abandon and entrust yourself to it, pursue where it goes,
and let it reach its end.
With nothing to abandon
and nothing to entrust,
why rush to hasten or delay in between?"
Yángzhū said:
"Bóchéng Zǐgāo did not benefit others with a single hair,
abandoned his state and hid in farming.
Dà Yǔ did not benefit himself,
and his body became partially withered.
The people of ancient times
would not give up a single hair to benefit the world,
nor would they accept the whole world to serve themselves.
If everyone does not give up a single hair,
and everyone does not benefit the world,
the world will be governed."
Qín Zǐ asked Yáng Zhū,
"If removing one of your hairs
could benefit the world,
would you do it?"
Yáng Zhū said,
"The world certainly cannot be benefited by a single hair."
Qín Zǐ said,
"Suppose it could,
would you do it?"
Yáng Zhū did not answer.
Qín Zǐ went out
and told Mèng Sūn Yáng.
Mèng Sūn Yáng said,
"You do not understand the Master's heart;
let me explain it.
If someone were to harm your skin to gain ten thousand gold pieces,
would you allow it?"
He said,
"I would."
Mèng Sūn Yáng said,
"If someone were to cut off one of your joints to gain a kingdom,
would you allow it?"
Qín Zǐ was silent for a while.
Mèng Sūn Yáng said,
"A hair is insignificant compared to the skin,
and the skin is insignificant compared to a joint.
It is clear.
Therefore, accumulating hairs forms skin,
and accumulating skin forms a joint.
A hair is certainly one ten-thousandth part of the body;
how can you take it lightly?"
Qín Zǐ said,
"I cannot answer you.
However, if I asked Lǎo Dān and Guān Yǐn your question,
your words would be correct;
if I asked Dà Yǔ and Mò Dí my question,
my words would be correct."
Mèng Sūn Yáng then turned and discussed other matters with his disciples.
Yáng Zhū said,
"The world attributes all good to Shùn, Yǔ, Zhōu, and Kǒng,
and all evil to Jié and Zhòu.
However, Shùn plowed in Héyáng,
made pottery in Léizé,
his body could not find a moment of peace,
his mouth and stomach could not enjoy delicious food;
he was not loved by his parents,
nor cherished by his siblings.
At the age of thirty,
he married without informing them.
When he received the abdication of Yáo,
he was already old,
and his wisdom had declined.
Shāng Jūn was not talented,
so he abdicated in favor of Yǔ,
and died in sorrow.
This is the ultimate misery of men chosen by Heaven.
Gǔn controlled the waters,
but his efforts were unsuccessful,
and he was executed on Yǔshān.
Yǔ continued his father's hated work,
focusing solely on land reclamation,
his son was not named,
he passed by his home without entering;
his body became emaciated,
his hands and feet calloused.
When he received the abdication of Shùn,
he lived in humble dwellings,
wore beautiful ceremonial robes and crowns,
and died in sorrow:
this is the worry and hardship of men chosen by Heaven.
After King Wǔ passed away,
King Chéng was young and weak,
and the Duke of Zhōu administered the government on behalf of the Son of Heaven.
The Duke of Shào was unhappy,
and rumors spread in the four kingdoms.
After living in the east for three years,
he executed his brother and exiled another,
barely saving himself,
and died in sorrow:
this is the danger and fear of men chosen by Heaven.
Kǒngzǐ elucidated the way of emperors and kings,
responding to the invitations of contemporary rulers,
he had trees felled in Sòng,
footprints erased in Wèi,
was impoverished in Shāng and Zhōu,
and besieged in Chén and Cài,
suffered humiliation from Jì Shì,
and was insulted by Yáng Hǔ,
and died in sorrow:
this is the haste and anxiety of men chosen by Heaven.
All these four sages
had no joy in life,
but have everlasting fame after death.
Fame
is certainly not something taken by the reality
Though praised, they do not know it;
though rewarded, they do not know it;
they are no different from tree stumps and clods of earth.
Jié relied on the wealth accumulated over generations,
and occupied the position of honor facing south,
his wisdom was enough to resist his subordinates,
his power was enough to shake the empire;
he indulged his senses,
and exhausted his thoughts and actions,
and died in happiness:
this is the indulgence of men chosen by Heaven.
Zhòu also relied on the wealth accumulated over generations,
and occupied the position of honor facing south;
his power was irresistible,
and his will was obeyed;
he indulged his passions in the Inclined Palace,
and indulged his desires in long nights;
he did not torment himself with propriety and righteousness,
and died in happiness, only to be executed:
this is the licentiousness of men chosen by Heaven.
Those two tyrants
had the joy of indulging their desires in life,
and were given names of foolish violence after death.
The reality, of course, is not given by the name,
though slandered, they do not know it;
though praised, they do not know it;
how are they different from tree stumps and clods of earth?
Those four sages, though praised by everyone,
suffered until the end,
and all returned to death.
Those two tyrants, though reviled by everyone,
enjoyed themselves until the end,
and also returned to death.
Yáng Zhū met with the King of Liáng
and said that governing the world was like manipulating something in the palm of one's hand.
The King of Liáng said,
"Sir, you cannot govern even one wife and one concubine,
nor cultivate a garden of three *mǔ*;
yet you say that governing the world is like manipulating something in the palm of one's hand;
how is that?"
He replied,
"Have you seen a shepherd?
A hundred sheep form a flock,
and a five-foot-tall boy can carry a whip and follow them,
and they go east when he wants them to go east,
and west when he wants them to go west.
But if Yáo were to lead one sheep,
and Shùn were to carry a whip and follow it,
they would not be able to move forward.
Moreover, I have heard that
a fish that can swallow a boat
does not swim in small streams;
a swan that flies high
does not gather in dirty ponds.
Why?
Because its goal is far away.
The *huángzhōng* and *dàlǚ* bells
cannot be used in the elaborate dances.
Why?
Because their tones are too grand.
One who governs great things does not govern small things,
and one who accomplishes great deeds does not accomplish small ones;
this is what I mean."
Yáng Zhū said,
"The events of high antiquity have vanished;
who can record them?
The events of the Three Sovereigns
seem to exist and yet not exist,
the events of the Five Emperors
seem like waking or dreaming,
the events of the Three Kings
are sometimes hidden and sometimes revealed;
I do not recognize one in a billion.
The things happening to oneself
are sometimes heard and sometimes seen;
I do not recognize one in ten thousand.
The things happening before one's eyes are sometimes remembered and sometimes forgotten;
I do not recognize one in a thousand.
From high antiquity to today,
the years are too many to count.
Since Fúxī, there have been over three hundred thousand years,
wise and foolish, beautiful and ugly, success and failure, right and wrong,
all have vanished;
the only difference is the speed.
To value the praise and blame of a moment,
and to torment one's spirit and body,
to seek a remaining name several hundred years after death,
is it enough to moisten dry bones?
What joy is there in life?"
Yáng Zhū said,
"Man resembles the patterns of heaven and earth,
and embodies the nature of the Five Constants,
he is the most intelligent of all living things.
Man,
his claws and teeth are not sufficient for defense,
his skin is not sufficient for self-protection,
his running is not sufficient to escape benefits and harms,
he has no feathers to ward off cold and heat,
he must rely on things for nourishment (nature),
and rely on wisdom instead of strength."
Therefore, what wisdom values is
valuing self-preservation;
what strength despises is
despising harming things.
However, the body is not something I possess;
having been born, I cannot but preserve it completely.
Things are not something I possess;
having them, I cannot abandon them.
The body is indeed the master of life,
and things are also the means to sustain life.
Even if preserving life completely (the body),
one cannot possess one's body;
even if not abandoning things,
one cannot possess things.
To possess things, to possess one's body,
is to selfishly appropriate the body of the world,
selfishly appropriate the things of the world.
One who does not selfishly appropriate the body of the world,
and does not selfishly appropriate the things of the world,
is perhaps only a sage!
To make the body public to the world,
to make things public to the world,
that is perhaps the ultimate person!
This is what is meant by 'reaching the ultimate'."
Yáng Zhū said:
"The reason why people cannot rest
is due to four things:
first is longevity (`shòu`),
second is fame (`míng`),
third is position (`wèi`),
fourth is wealth (`huò`).
Having these four,
one fears ghosts,
fears people,
fears authority,
fears punishment:
these are called fugitive people.
They can be killed or kept alive,
their fate is controlled externally.
If one does not resist fate,
why envy longevity?
If one does not value nobility,
why envy fame?
If one does not desire power,
why envy position?
If one is not greedy for riches,
why envy wealth?
These are called compliant people.
They have no equal in the world,
their fate is controlled internally.
Therefore, there is a saying:
If people do not marry and seek office,
half of their desires are lost;
if people do not clothe and feed themselves,
the way of ruler and subject ceases.
A saying from Zhōu goes:
'A peasant can be killed while sitting.'
Coming out in the morning and entering at night,
they consider it the constancy of their nature;
sipping bean broth and eating coarse vegetables,
they consider it the height of flavor;
their muscles are coarse and thick,
their tendons are tense and tight;
if one day they are placed in soft fur and silk tents,
offered fine grains, meat, orchids, and tangerines,
their heart will ache and their body will be troubled,
internal heat will arise, and they will become ill.
If the rulers of Shāng and Lǔ shared the same land as a peasant,
they would also be exhausted in less than an hour.
Therefore, what rustic people are comfortable with,
what rustic people find beautiful,
they say there is nothing in the world that surpasses it.
In the past, in the state of Sòng, there was a farmer
who always wore hemp and ramie,
barely enough to get through the winter.
When spring arrived and he began working in the fields,
he basked in the sun,
not knowing that the world had broad mansions and deep rooms,
cotton padding and fox furs.
He turned to his wife and said:
'The warmth of basking in the sun,
no one knows;
if I offer it to our ruler,
I will receive a great reward.'
A wealthy man in the village told him:
'In the past, there was a man who praised good wild beans,
sweet hemp stalks, celery, and duckweed,
boasting about them to the local gentry.
The local gentry took them and tasted them,
they stung the mouth,
caused pain in the stomach,
everyone laughed and resented him,
and the man was greatly ashamed.
You are like this.'
Yáng Zhū said:
"Luxurious houses, beautiful clothes,
rich flavors, and lovely appearances.
Having these four,
why seek anything outside?
To have these and still seek outside,
is to have a nature without satisfaction.
A nature without satisfaction
is a parasite on Yīn and Yáng.
Loyalty is not enough to secure the ruler,
it is only enough to endanger oneself;
righteousness is not enough to benefit others,
it is only enough to harm life.
Securing the superior does not depend on loyalty,
and the name of loyalty is extinguished;
benefiting others does not depend on righteousness,
and the name of righteousness is cut off.
Ruler and subject both secure,
things and self both benefit,
this is the ancient way.
Yù Zǐ said:
'One who abandons fame has no worries.'
Lǎo Zǐ said:
'Fame is a guest of substance.'
Yet the leisurely ones pursue fame without end.
Is fame truly impossible to abandon?
Is fame truly impossible to treat as a guest?
Now, having fame brings honor and glory,
losing fame brings lowliness and disgrace.
Honor and glory bring ease and pleasure,
lowliness and disgrace bring worry and suffering.
Worry and suffering
violate nature,
ease and pleasure
accord with nature.
This is where substance is tied.
How can fame be abandoned?
How can fame be treated as a guest?
But I hate those who cling to fame and burden substance.
To cling to fame and burden substance
will lead to worrying about the unsalvageable danger and ruin;
how can it be merely a matter of ease, pleasure, worry, and suffering?"
Zǐ Lièzǐ studied with Húqiū Zǐlín.
Húqiū Zǐlín said:
"If you know how to hold the rear,
then you can talk about preserving the self."
Lièzǐ said:
"I wish to hear about holding the rear."
He said:
"Look at your shadow,
and you will understand it."
Lièzǐ looked and observed his shadow:
if the form is crooked, then the shadow is bent;
if the form is straight, then the shadow is upright.
Therefore, crookedness and straightness follow the form and are not in the shadow;
bending and stretching depend on things and are not in me.
This is called holding the rear and being in front.
Guānyǐn said to Zǐ Lièzǐ:
"If words are beautiful, then the echo is beautiful;
if words are evil, then the echo is evil;
if the body is tall, then the shadow is long;
if the body is short, then the shadow is short.
Fame is
an echo,
conduct is
a shadow.
Therefore, it is said:
be careful with your words,
and there will be a response;
be careful with your conduct,
and there will be a consequence.
Therefore, the sage sees the outflow to know the inflow,
observes the past to know the future;
this is the principle by which he knows beforehand.
The measure is in oneself,
the verification is in others.
If people love me,
I must love them;
if people hate me,
I must hate them.
Tāng and Wǔ loved the world,
therefore they became kings;
Jié and Zhòu hated the world,
therefore they perished;
this is what is verified.
To have both measure and verification clear yet not follow the Way,
is like going out without using the door,
traveling without following the path.
To seek benefit in this way,
is it not difficult?
Try observing the virtues of Shénnóng and Yǒuyán,
verifying them in the books of Yú, Xià, Shāng, and Zhōu,
measuring them against the words of legalists and wise men,
and there has never been a case of survival, ruin, abandonment, or rise that did not come from this Way."
Yán Huī said:
"The reason for asking about the Way is to become rich.
Now, obtaining a pearl is also riches,
what use is the Way?"
Zǐ Lièzǐ said:
"Jié and Zhòu valued profit and despised the Way,
and therefore perished.
Fortunately, I have not yet spoken to you about it."
A person without righteousness is only concerned with eating;
he is like a chicken or a dog.
To forcefully consume and lack horns,
where the victor dictates the rules,
is the way of birds and beasts.
To be a chicken, dog, bird, or beast,
yet desire others to respect oneself,
is impossible.
If people do not respect you,
then danger and disgrace will befall you."
Liè Zǐ learned archery
and hit the target.
He asked Guān Yǐn Zǐ about it.
Guān Yǐn Zǐ said:
"Do you know the reason you hit the target?"
He replied:
"I do not know."
Guān Yǐn Zǐ said:
"Not yet."
He withdrew and practiced.
After three years,
he reported to Guān Yǐn Zǐ again.
Guān Yǐn Zǐ said:
"Do you know the reason you hit the target?"
Liè Zǐ said:
"I know it."
Guān Yǐn Zǐ said:
"Acceptable;
guard it and do not lose it.
It is not only archery;
governing a state and cultivating oneself
are both the same.
Therefore, the sage does not examine existence or extinction,
but examines the reason for them."
Liè Zǐ said:
"One with flourishing looks is arrogant,
one with flourishing strength is energetic,
they cannot be spoken to about the Dao.
Therefore, one does not speak of the Dao to those who are not white-haired,
let alone practice it.
Therefore, if one strives on one's own, no one will advise them.
If no one advises them,
then they will be isolated and without assistance.
The wise entrust tasks to others,
therefore they do not decline with age,
and their wisdom is inexhaustible and not disordered.
Therefore, the difficulty in governing a state
lies in recognizing the worthy, not in considering oneself worthy."
A man of Sòng made a Chǔ leaf of jade for his ruler,
taking three years to complete it.
The sharpness, stalks, and branches
and fine hairs and abundant luster
were such that when mixed among real Chǔ leaves,
it could not be distinguished.
This man then used his skill to gain food in the state of Sòng.
Zǐ Liè Zǐ heard of it and said:
"If Heaven and Earth created things,
taking three years to make a single leaf,
then there would be few leaves in the world.
Therefore, the sage relies on the transformative power of the Dao and does not rely on clever skill."
Zǐ Liè Zǐ was impoverished,
and his face showed signs of hunger.
A guest told Zhèng Zǐyáng about it,
saying:
"Liè Yǔkòu is probably a man of the Dao;
living in your country and being impoverished,
is it not that you do not favor men of virtue?"
Zhèng Zǐyáng immediately ordered an official to send him grain.
Zǐ Liè Zǐ came out
to see the messenger,
bowed twice and declined.
The messenger left.
Zǐ Liè Zǐ entered,
and his wife, seeing him, beat her chest and said:
"I have heard that the wives and children of those who have the Dao
all enjoy leisure and happiness.
Now we have a hungry look,
and the ruler, taking pity, sends you food.
You do not accept it;
is this not fate?"
Zǐ Liè Zǐ smiled and said to her:
"The ruler does not know me himself.
He sent me grain based on the words of others;
when he comes to blame me,
he will also do so based on the words of others.
This is why I did not accept it."
In the end,
the people indeed caused trouble
and killed Zǐyáng.
Shī Shì of Lǔ had two sons,
one who loved learning
and one who loved military affairs.
The one who loved learning used his skills to seek an audience with the Marquis of Qí;
the Marquis of Qí accepted him and made him a tutor to the young nobles.
The one who loved military affairs went to Chǔ,
using his methods to seek an audience with the King of Chǔ;
the King of Chǔ was pleased with him
and made him a military officer.
Their family became wealthy,
and their relatives were honored with titles.
Méng Shì, a neighbor of Shī Shì,
also had two sons,
who pursued the same professions,
but they were troubled by poverty.
Envying the possessions of Shī Shì,
they asked them for the method of advancement.
The two sons truthfully told the Méng family.
One son of the Méng family went to Qín,
using his skills to seek an audience with the King of Qín.
The King of Qín said:
"These days, the nobles are contending with force,
focusing only on military affairs and food.
If I use benevolence and righteousness to govern my state,
it would be the path to destruction."
He was castrated and released.
One son went to Wèi,
using his methods to seek an audience with the Marquis of Wèi.
The Marquis of Wèi said:
"My state is weak
and caught between large states.
I serve the large states,
and I comfort the small states;
this is the way to seek peace.
If I rely on military power,
destruction can be expected.
If I send him back whole
to another state,
the trouble he would cause me would not be light."
He had him mutilated and sent back to Lǔ.
Having returned,
the father and sons of the Méng family beat their chests and blamed the Shī family.
The Shī family said:
"Generally, those who gain the time flourish,
and those who lose the time perish.
Your methods are the same as ours,
but your success is different;
you have lost the time,
not that your actions are wrong.
Furthermore, there is no constant right principle in the world,
and no constant wrong in affairs.
What was previously used
may now be discarded;
what is now discarded
may be used later.
This use and non-use
have no fixed right or wrong.
Seizing opportunities and meeting the times,
responding to affairs without a fixed method
belongs to wisdom.
If wisdom is insufficient,
then even if one is as learned as Kǒng Qiū
and as skilled as Lǚ Shàng,
where would they go without encountering difficulty?"
The Méng family father and sons calmly showed no resentment,
saying:
"We understand.
Do not repeat yourself!"
Duke Wén of Jìn was going to a meeting
and wanted to attack Wèi.
Gōngzǐ Chú looked up to the sky and laughed.
The Duke asked why he laughed.
He said:
"I laugh at a neighbor who was sending his wife
to a lover's house,
and on the way, saw a woman picking mulberry leaves,
was pleased and spoke to her.
Then he looked back at his wife,
and there was someone beckoning to her.
I secretly laughed at this."
The Duke understood
his words and stopped.
He led the army back,
and before they arrived, someone had attacked his northern borders.
The state of Jìn suffered from thieves.
There was a man named Xì Yōng
who could see the appearance of thieves,
observing the space between their eyebrows and eyelashes to discern their intentions.
The Marquis of Jìn had him identify thieves,
and he never missed a single one.
The Marquis of Jìn was greatly pleased
and told Zhào Wén Zǐ, saying:
"I have obtained one person,
and the thieves of the entire country will be eliminated because of him;
why use many?"
Wén Zǐ said:
"My lord relies on surveillance to catch thieves,
the thieves will not be eliminated,
and Xì Yōng will certainly not die a natural death."
Soon after, the thieves plotted, saying:
"The reason we are in trouble is Xì Yōng."
They then conspired and murdered him.
The Marquis of Jìn heard of it and was greatly alarmed,
immediately summoning Wén Zǐ and telling him, saying:
"It is as you said,
Xì Yōng is dead!
Then what method should we use to catch thieves?"
Wén Zǐ said:
"There is a saying in Zhōu:
'He who clearly sees the fish in the deep is inauspicious;
he who cleverly anticipates hidden things will suffer calamity.'
If the ruler wishes to have no thieves,
it would be best not to promote and appoint the worthy;
let teachings be clear above,
and transformation be practiced below;
when the people have a sense of shame,
why would they steal?"
As a result, with Suí Huì knowing the government,
the groups of thieves fled to Qín.
When Kǒngzǐ returned from Wèi to Lǔ,
he rested his carriage by the Hé bridge and observed.
There was a waterfall thirty *rèn* high,
with a circular flow of ninety *lǐ*,
where fish and turtles could not swim,
and soft-shelled turtles and alligators could not dwell.
There was a man
who was about to brave it.
Kǒngzǐ sent someone along the bank to stop him, saying:
"This is a waterfall thirty *rèn* high,
with a circular flow of ninety *lǐ*,
where fish and turtles cannot swim,
and soft-shelled turtles and alligators cannot dwell.
Do you think it can be easily crossed?"
The man did not take it to heart,
and proceeded to cross and emerge.
Kǒngzǐ asked him, saying:
"Are you skillful?
Do you have a technique?
What is it that allows you to enter and emerge?"
The man replied, saying:
"When I entered,
I first relied on loyalty and trustworthiness;
and when I emerged,
I again followed with loyalty and trustworthiness.
Loyalty and trustworthiness placed my body in the currents,
and I dared not use my personal feelings.
The reason I was able to enter and emerge again
is because of this."
Kǒngzǐ said to his disciples:
"Remember this, my students!
Even water can be approached safely with loyalty and trustworthiness,
how much more so with people?"
Bái Gōng asked Kǒngzǐ, saying:
"Can one speak subtly to people?"
Kǒngzǐ did not answer.
Bái Gōng asked, saying:
"What if one throws a stone into the water?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The skilled divers of Wú can retrieve it."
He said:
"What if one throws water into water?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When the Zī and Miǎn rivers merge,
Yì Yá can taste and know it."
Bái Gōng said:
"Is it truly impossible to speak subtly to people?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Why would it be impossible?
It's only about knowing how to speak!
Knowing how to speak
is not about speaking with words.
Those who fight over fish get wet,
those who chase beasts hurry;
they do not enjoy it.
Therefore, the ultimate words go beyond words,
and the ultimate action is non-action.
What shallow knowledge disputes
are trifles."
Bái Gōng, having no other recourse,
then died in the bathroom.
Zhào Xiāngzǐ sent the newly appointed Mù Zǐ to attack Dí,
and he was victorious,
capturing Zuǒrén and Zhōngrén.
He sent a messenger to report to him.
Xiāngzǐ was eating and had a worried look.
Those around him said:
"Two cities have fallen in a single morning;
this is what people rejoice over;
now you, sir, have a worried look.
Why is that?"
Xiāngzǐ said:
"Even the great rivers and streams
do not last more than three days;
violent winds and storms do not last all morning,
and the sun is not at its zenith for long.
Now, the virtue and conduct of the Zhào clan
have not been accumulated;
with two cities falling in a single morning,
ruin may befall us!"
Kǒngzǐ heard of this and said:
"The Zhào clan will prosper!
Worry is the means of prosperity,
while joy is the means of ruin.
Victory is not the difficult part;
maintaining it is the difficult part.
Wise rulers use this to maintain victory,
therefore their blessings extend to later generations.
Qí, Chǔ, Wú, and Yuè all once achieved victory,
but ultimately met with ruin,
because they did not understand how to maintain victory.
Only rulers who follow the Dao are able to maintain victory."
Kǒngzǐ's strength
was enough to lift the gates of a country,
but he did not wish to be known for his strength.
Mòzǐ defended against sieges,
and Gōngshū Bān submitted,
but he did not wish to be known for his military expertise.
Therefore, those skilled at maintaining victory
use strength as weakness.
There was a man of Sòng who was fond of practicing benevolence and righteousness,
and did so tirelessly for three generations.
For no reason, a black cow in his family gave birth to a white calf,
and he asked Kǒngzǐ about it.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"This is auspicious;
use it as an offering to the High God."
After a year,
his father became blind for no reason.
His cow again gave birth to a white calf,
and his father again ordered his son to ask Kǒngzǐ.
The son said:
"I asked him before, and we lost our sight;
why ask again?"
His father said:
"The words of a sage may seem contradictory at first but will later align with events.
The matter is not yet resolved,
so let us ask again."
The son again asked Kǒngzǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is auspicious."
He again instructed him on the sacrifice.
The son returned and reported the instructions.
His father said:
"Do as Kǒngzǐ says."
After a year,
his son also became blind for no reason.
Later, Chǔ attacked Sòng,
and besieged the city.
The people exchanged children and ate them,
and broke bones to cook.
The able-bodied men all mounted the city walls to fight,
and more than half of them died.
This man and his son, because of their illness,
were both spared.
When the siege was lifted, their illnesses both recovered.
There was a certain Lán Zǐ of Sòng
who sought an audience with Yuán Jūn of Sòng with his skills.
Yuán Jūn of Sòng summoned him and made him appear. His skill
involved using two branches, twice as long as his body,
attached to his shins,
running and galloping in unison,
juggling seven swords,
taking turns leaping over them,
with five swords constantly in the air.
Yuán Jūn was greatly astonished
and immediately bestowed gold and silk upon him.
There was another Lán Zǐ who was also skilled in entertaining performances,
and upon hearing of this,
also sought an audience with Yuán Jūn.
Yuán Jūn was greatly angered and said:
"In the past, there was someone with unusual skills who sought an audience with me.
His skill was useless,
but it happened to coincide with me being in a joyful mood,
so I bestowed gold and silk upon him.
He must have heard of this and advanced,
again hoping for my reward."
He had him arrested and considered executing him,
but released him after a month.
Duke Mù of Qín said to Bólè:
"You are old now;
do you have any descendants who can be employed to find horses?"
Bólè replied:
"Fine horses
can be described in terms of their physique and bone structure.
Those who can identify the horses of the world
seem to disappear and vanish,
as if lost or gone.
Such horses leave dust behind and erase hoofprints.
My sons are all of lower talent;
they can be told about fine horses,
but they cannot be told about the horses of the world.
I have someone who shares the burden of ropes and gathers firewood with me,
named Jiǔ Fānggāo;
his judgment of horses
is not inferior to mine.
Please see him."
Duke Mù saw him and
sent him to look for a horse.
After three months, he returned
and reported, saying:
"I have already found it;
it is in Shāqiū."
Duke Mù said:
"What kind of horse is it?"
He replied:
"A female and yellow one."
He sent someone to fetch it, and it was
a male and black one.
Duke Mù was displeased,
summoned Bólè and said to him:
"It is a failure!
The one you sent to look for the horse!
He cannot even distinguish color, appearance, female, or male,
so how can he know anything about horses?"
Bólè sighed deeply and said:
"Has it come to this!
This is precisely why I am worth thousands as a subject but countless otherwise.
What Gāo observes
is the heavenly mechanism;
he grasps the essence and forgets the rough,
focuses on the internal and forgets the external,
sees what he sees
and does not see what he does not see,
looks at what he looks at
and omits what he does not look at.
What Gāo examines
is something more valuable than the horse itself."
When the horse arrived,
it was indeed the finest horse in the land.
King Zhuāng of Chǔ asked Zhān Hé:
"How should I govern the state?"
Zhān Hé replied:
"I am skilled in governing myself but not in governing the state."
King Zhuāng of Chǔ said:
"I am fortunate to serve the ancestral temples and the altars of the state,
and I wish to learn how to protect them."
Zhān Hé replied:
"I have never heard of a case where the self was well-governed but the state was in chaos,
nor have I ever heard of a case where the self was in chaos but the state was well-governed.
Therefore, the root lies in the self,
and I dare not answer with the branches."
The King of Chǔ said:
"Good."
The old man of Húqiū said to Sūn Shū'áo:
"People have three grievances;
do you know them?"
Sūn Shū'áo said:
"What are they?"
He replied:
"Those with high rank are envied;
those with great power are disliked by the ruler;
those with generous salaries are resented."
Sūn Shū'áo said:
"As my rank increases,
my ambition decreases;
as my power increases,
my mind becomes more humble;
as my salary increases,
my generosity expands.
Can I avoid the three grievances in this way?"
Is that possible?"
Sūn Shū'áo fell ill, and as he was about to die,
he warned his son, saying:
"The king has repeatedly offered me a fief,
but I have not accepted it.
When I die,
the king will grant you a fief.
You must not accept a profitable land!
Between Chǔ and Yuè
there is a place called Qǐnqiū;
this land is unfavorable and has a very bad name.
The people of Chǔ are superstitious about ghosts, and the people of Yuè are superstitious about omens,
so only this place can be possessed for a long time."
Sūn Shū'áo died,
and the king indeed offered his son a beautiful piece of land.
The son declined to accept it;
he requested Qǐnqiū,
and it was granted to him.
To this day, he has not lost it.
Niú Quē was
a great Confucian scholar from Shàngdì.
He was traveling to Hándān
when he encountered bandits in the midst of Ǒushā.
They took all his clothing and carriage,
and he walked away at a leisurely pace.
Looking at him,
he had a joyful and carefree expression.
The bandits chased after him and asked the reason.
He said:
"A gentleman does not harm what he nurtures for the sake of what nurtures him."
The bandits said:
"Ah!
How virtuous he is!"
Then they said to each other:
"With his virtue,
if he goes to see the ruler of Zhào,
he will surely expose us,
and we will be in trouble.
We should kill him."
So they chased after him together and killed him.
When the people of Yān heard of this,
they gathered their families and warned each other,
saying:
"If you encounter bandits, be like Niú Quē from Shàngdì!"
They all accepted the teaching.
Soon after, his younger brother went to Qín.
When he arrived at Quēxià,
he indeed encountered bandits;
remembering his brother's warning,
he struggled with the bandits.
Since he was not as strong,
he chased after them and begged them for the goods with humble words.
The bandits angrily said:
"We spared your life out of generosity,
but you keep chasing us relentlessly,
leaving a clear trail.
Since we are already bandits,
where is benevolence to be found?"
So they killed him
and also harmed four or five members of his group.
Yú Shì was
a wealthy man from Liáng.
His family was prosperous and thriving,
with limitless money and silk,
and incalculable wealth.
He ascended a high building,
overlooking a major road,
arranged music and displayed wine,
and played bó on the upper floor.
Knights-errant followed each other as they walked.
Those playing bó on the upper floor shot,
and a bright arrow hit the target,
turning over two ivory fish
and laughing.
A kite happened to drop its rotten rat and hit them.
The knights-errant said to each other:
"The Yú family has enjoyed wealth and pleasure for a long time
and always has an attitude of looking down on people.
We have not invaded or offended him,
yet he humiliates us with a rotten rat.
If we do not avenge this,
we will not be able to establish our trustworthiness in the world.
Let us join forces with you,
lead our followers,
and surely destroy his family to be equal."
They all agreed.
On the night of the appointed day,
they gathered a crowd and stockpiled weapons
to attack the Yú family,
and greatly destroyed his family.
There was a man in the east
named Yuán Jīngmù,
who was about to go somewhere
but was starving on the road.
A bandit from Húfù named Qiū
saw him and offered him a pot of food to nourish him.
Yuán Jīngmù could see only after three mouthfuls
and said:
"What kind of person are you?"
He said:
"I am Qiū, a man from Húfù."
Yuán Jīngmù said:
"Alas! Are you not a bandit?
Why are you feeding me?
It is against my principles to eat your food."
He supported himself on the ground with both hands and vomited,
but nothing came out.
He coughed and coughed, and then collapsed to the ground and died.
The people of Húfù were indeed bandits,
but the food was not stolen.
Because the person was a bandit,
he considered the food to be stolen and dared not eat it.
This is a case of losing sight of the correspondence between name and reality.
Zhù Lìshū served Gǔ Áogōng.
Thinking that he was not appreciated, he left
and lived by the sea.
In the summer, he ate water caltrops and water chestnuts,
and in the winter, he ate acorns and chestnuts.
When Gǔ Áogōng was in trouble,
Zhù Lìshū bid farewell to his friends and went to die for him.
His friend said,
"You thought yourself not understood,
and so you left.
Now you are going to die for it.
This is to make no distinction between understanding and not understanding."
Zhù Lìshū said,
"Not so.
Because I thought myself not understood,
I left.
Now, if I die,
it is indeed because I am not understood.
I will die
to shame later generations of rulers who do not understand their ministers."
To die when understood,
and not to die when not understood,
this is to follow the straight path.
Zhù Lìshū can be said to have resented to the point of forgetting himself.
Yáng Zhū said:
"Benefits given out will surely return;
resentments sent out will bring harm back.
What originates here and finds response outside is only invitation;
therefore, the worthy are cautious of what they put forth."
Yángzǐ's neighbor lost a sheep,
and having gathered his clan,
he also asked Yángzǐ's servant to pursue it.
Yángzǐ said:
"Alas!
A lost sheep, why so many pursuers?"
The neighbor said:
"Many crossroads."
Having returned,
he was asked:
"Did you recover the sheep?"
He said:
"It was lost."
He was asked:
"How was it lost?"
He said:
"Among the crossroads there were even more crossroads.
I did not know where to go,
and so I returned."
Yángzǐ looked grieved and changed countenance,
remaining silent for a long time,
and not smiling for the entire day.
His disciples found it strange
and asked:
"Sheep are base animals,
and not even the master's own.
Why this loss of speech and laughter?"
Yángzǐ did not answer.
The disciples did not receive instruction.
The disciple Mèng Sūnyáng went out
and told Xīndūzǐ.
Another day, Xīndūzǐ entered with Mèng Sūnyáng and asked,
"Once there were three brothers
who traveled between Qí and Lǔ,
studying with the same teacher,
advancing in the way of benevolence and righteousness before returning home.
Their father asked:
'What is the way of benevolence and righteousness like?'
The eldest said:
'Benevolence and righteousness cause me to cherish my life before my reputation.'
The second said:
'Benevolence and righteousness cause me to sacrifice my life to achieve reputation.'
The youngest said:
'Benevolence and righteousness cause me to preserve both life and reputation.'
These three approaches contradict each other,
yet all come from Confucianism.
Which is right and which is wrong?"
Yángzǐ said:
"There are those who live by the river,
accustomed to the water,
brave in swimming,
who operate boats for ferrying,
providing for the livelihood of a hundred mouths.
Those who wrap up provisions and go to study swimming become a crowd,
but those who drown are nearly half.
They originally learn to swim, not to drown,
yet the benefit and harm are like this.
What do you consider right and wrong?"
Xīndūzǐ remained silent and left.
Mèng Sūnyáng reproached him, saying:
"Why did you ask so circuitously,
and the master answer so obliquely?
My confusion has only deepened."
Xīndūzǐ said:
"The great road loses sheep due to many forks;
scholars lose life due to many pursuits.
The principles learned are not inherently different,
not inherently non-identical,
yet the outcomes vary so greatly.
Only by returning to the same origin,
can one account for loss and gain.
You have long been in the master's school,
learning the master's way,
and yet you do not understand the master's allusions.
Alas!"
Yáng Zhū's younger brother, Bù,
went out wearing white clothes.
It rained,
so he took off the white clothes
and returned wearing black clothes.
His dog did not recognize him
and barked at him.
Yáng Bù was angry and about to strike it.
Yáng Zhū said:
"Do not strike it.
You are just like that.
If you had made your dog go out white and come back black,
could you have helped but find it strange?"
Yáng Zhū said:
"Do good without seeking fame, and fame will follow;
do not plan for profit with fame, and profit will come;
do not plan to contend for profit, and contention will reach you;
therefore, the gentleman must be cautious in doing good."
In the past, someone claimed to know the way to immortality.
The ruler of Yān sent someone to learn it,
but was unsuccessful,
and the claimant was killed.
The ruler of Yān was furious, and his envoy
was about to be punished.
A favored minister advised:
"What people worry about most is death;
what they value most is life.
He himself lost his life,
how could he enable the ruler not to die?"
So he was not punished.
There was a man from Qí who also wanted to learn this way,
but upon hearing of the claimant's death,
he clutched his breast and regretted it.
Fùzǐ heard of it and laughed, saying:
"He desired to learn immortality,
but the man is already dead
and he still regrets it.
This is not knowing how to learn."
Húzǐ said:
"Fùzǐ's words are wrong.
There are cases of people having a method but being unable to practice it;
there are also cases of being able to practice it but lacking the method.
There was a man from Wèi skilled in calculations.
Nearing death,
he used analogies to explain it to his son,
but his son remembered his words without being able to practice them.
When others asked him,
he told them what his father had said.
The questioner used his words and practiced the method,
without differing from his father.
If so,
why could the dead not speak of the art of living?"
The people of Hándān
presented doves to Jiǎnzi on the first day of the new year.
Jiǎnzi was greatly pleased
and rewarded them generously.
A guest asked the reason.
Jiǎnzi said:
"Releasing life on New Year's Day
shows kindness."
The guest said:
"The people know that you want to release them,
so they compete to capture them,
and many die.
If you truly want to save them,
you should forbid the people from capturing them.
Capturing them and then releasing them
is not enough to compensate for the harm done."
Jiǎnzi said:
"That is so."
Tián of Qí held a sacrifice in his courtyard,
with a thousand retainers as guests.
In the middle of the gathering, someone presented fish and geese.
Tián looked at them
and sighed, saying:
"Heaven is generous to the people!
It grows the five grains,
and produces fish and birds
for their use."
The guests echoed him in unison.
The son of the Bào family, twelve years old,
was present at the gathering.
He stepped forward and said:
"What you say is not right.
Heaven and earth and the myriad things
are born alongside us, of the same kind.
Among things of the same kind, there is no high or low,
but they control each other merely by differences in size, intelligence, and strength,
and devour each other in turn;
they are not born for each other.
People take what is edible and eat it;
how could Heaven have originally produced it for people's sake?
Moreover, mosquitoes bite skin,
tigers and wolves eat meat—
did Heaven originally produce people for mosquitoes, or meat for tigers and wolves?"
In Qí (齊) there was a poor man who
constantly begged in the city.
The city dwellers were annoyed by his frequent begging,
and no one gave him anything.
So he went to the stables of the Tián (田) family,
worked as a servant for the horse doctor, and begged for food.
People in the town ridiculed him, saying,
"Working for a horse doctor for food,
aren't you ashamed?"
The beggar said,
"Nothing in the world is more shameful than begging.
If begging isn't shameful,
how could working for a horse doctor be?"
A man of Sòng (宋) was wandering on the road,
and found a contract someone had lost.
He took it home and hid it,
secretly counting its entries.
He told his neighbor,
"I can expect to be rich soon."
A man had a withered wútóng (梧桐) tree.
His neighbor's father said that a withered wútóng tree was unlucky,
so the neighbor quickly chopped it down.
The neighbor's father then asked to have it as firewood.
The man was displeased, saying,
"The neighbor's father only wanted firewood
and taught me to cut it down.
Living next to someone like this is
dangerous. How can I?"
A man lost his axe
and suspected his neighbor's son.
He watched his gait,
and it was like someone stealing an axe.
His expression
was like someone stealing an axe,
his speech
was like someone stealing an axe;
his every action and attitude
was like someone stealing an axe.
Suddenly, he dug in the valley and found his axe.
The next day, he saw his neighbor's son again,
and his every action and attitude
was no longer like someone stealing an axe.
Bái Gōng Shèng (白公勝) was worried about rebellion.
He left the court and stood up,
leaning on his staff.
The metal point went up and pierced his chin,
blood flowed to the ground, but he didn't notice.
The people of Zhèng (鄭) heard of this and said,
"If he can forget his chin,
what won't he forget?"
When the mind is focused on something,
one's feet might stumble on tree stumps and holes,
one's head might bump into trees,
and one wouldn't even notice.
Once, a man of Qí (齊) wanted gold.
Early in the morning, he put on his clothes and hat and went to the market,
went to the place where someone was selling gold,
grabbed the gold and left.
The officer caught him,
and asked,
"Everyone was there,
why did you grab someone else's gold?"
He replied,
"When I took the gold,
I didn't see people,
I only saw the gold."
